Short answer: classic Outlook for Windows (2007 to 2021, and Microsoft 365 desktop) renders HTML email with Microsoft Word's engine, not a browser. Word ignores much of modern CSS, so layouts built with divs, flexbox, margins or background images fall apart. The fix is to build emails the way Word understands them: nested tables, inline styles, fixed widths, and Outlook-only code wrapped in MSO conditional comments.

This guide covers the most common Outlook problems we fix every week at MailStora, what causes each one and the exact change that solves it. If you would rather hand it over, our Outlook email rendering fix service tests your email in 50+ clients and fixes it, usually within 24 to 48 hours.

Why Outlook Breaks HTML Emails

Most email clients (Gmail, Apple Mail, iOS Mail, Outlook on the web and the new Outlook) use a browser engine to display email. Classic Outlook for Windows does not. It uses Word, which supports only a limited, older set of HTML and CSS. That causes the same symptoms again and again:

  • Columns stacking or collapsing, and layouts stretching to full width
  • Rounded buttons turning into plain links or square boxes
  • Background images disappearing
  • Extra gaps between images, or text lines that are too tall
  • Images showing at their original, huge size
  • Web fonts replaced by Times New Roman

The new Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the web behave much more like a browser, but many companies still run classic Outlook, so your email has to work in both. If you are not sure which version your readers use, our comparison of new Outlook vs classic Outlook rendering explains the differences.

1. Use Tables for Layout, Not Divs

Word does not reliably support float, flex, grid or max-width on divs. Build the structure with tables instead:

  • Wrap the email in a 100% width table, with a centred inner table 600 to 640 pixels wide.
  • Put each section in its own table row, and each column in its own table cell.
  • Set width as an HTML attribute as well as in CSS, because Word reads the attribute.
  • Add role="presentation" so screen readers do not announce layout tables.

For responsive multi-column layouts, the common pattern is a "ghost table": columns are inline-block divs for modern clients, and an Outlook-only table wrapped around them in conditional comments keeps them side by side in Word.

2. Target Outlook With MSO Conditional Comments

Outlook reads a special comment syntax that every other client ignores. It is the cleanest way to give Outlook its own code:

<!--[if mso]>
  <table role="presentation" width="600"><tr><td>
<![endif]-->
  ...your normal HTML...
<!--[if mso]>
  </td></tr></table>
<![endif]-->

Use it for fixed-width wrappers, Outlook-only fonts, and the VML elements below. Use <!--[if !mso]><!--> to hide code from Outlook.

Watch out: some ESP editors and minifiers strip HTML comments, which silently removes your Outlook fixes. Check the final sent code, not just your source file.

3. Make Buttons Bulletproof

A button made from a padded link with border-radius becomes a plain text link in Outlook, because Word ignores padding on inline elements. Two reliable fixes:

  • Table-cell buttons: put the background colour and padding on a table cell, and the link inside it. It stays square in Outlook but always looks like a button.
  • VML buttons: use a v:roundrect element inside an MSO conditional comment for Outlook, and a normal styled link for every other client. This keeps rounded corners in Outlook too.

A simple table-cell button:

<table role="presentation" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr><td bgcolor="#1a73e8" style="padding:14px 28px; border-radius:6px;">
    <a href="https://example.com" style="color:#ffffff; text-decoration:none; font-weight:bold;">Shop now</a>
  </td></tr>
</table>

For a fuller walkthrough, see our guide to bulletproof email buttons.

4. Fix Background Images With VML

CSS background images do not display in classic Outlook. For hero sections with text over an image, add a VML v:rect with a v:fill of the image inside an MSO comment, and keep the CSS background for other clients. Always set a solid bgcolor fallback so the text stays readable if images are blocked.

VML needs a fixed width and height in points or pixels, so plan the hero at a set size. If the design needs the image to scale fluidly, it is often simpler to use a plain image with live text below it. Our step-by-step post on Outlook background images with VML has the full code.

5. Stop Images Rendering at Full Size

Outlook ignores CSS widths on images and uses the file's real size. A 1200-pixel image exported at 2x for retina screens will burst out of a 600-pixel layout.

  • Always set the width attribute on every img, for example width="600", as well as style="width:100%; max-width:600px; height:auto;".
  • Add display:block and border:0 to remove the small gap Outlook adds under images.
  • Write meaningful alt text, because Outlook blocks images by default for many users.

Our post on email images not showing covers blocking, hosting and file type issues.

6. Control Spacing and Line Height

  • Use padding on table cells for spacing. Word ignores margins on many elements and handles padding on divs badly.
  • Add mso-line-height-rule: exactly; next to line-height so Outlook does not add extra space to lines of text.
  • Reset paragraph margins with margin:0 and add spacing through padding instead.
  • Set border-collapse: collapse and mso-table-lspace/rspace: 0pt on tables to remove hairline gaps.

7. Fix Blurry or Oversized Layouts on High-DPI Screens

On Windows machines set to 120 DPI (125% scaling), Outlook can scale images and widths inconsistently. Add the Office settings block in the head so Outlook uses 96 DPI for layout:

<!--[if mso]>
<noscript><xml><o:OfficeDocumentSettings>
  <o:PixelsPerInch>96</o:PixelsPerInch>
</o:OfficeDocumentSettings></xml></noscript>
<![endif]-->

8. Give Web Fonts a Safe Fallback

Classic Outlook does not load web fonts and may fall back to Times New Roman. List a system font in every font stack, for example font-family: 'Inter', Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;, and add an Outlook-only rule that forces Arial on text elements inside an MSO conditional style block.

9. Check Dark Mode in Outlook

Outlook's dark mode can invert background and text colours. Avoid pure black and white where you can, use transparent PNG logos with a subtle outline or a light version, and test with real dark mode previews. Our guide to email testing and Outlook fixes explains how we test light and dark mode side by side, and our dark mode email design post covers the design side.

10. Test in Real Outlook Versions Before You Send

Fixing Outlook without testing is guesswork. Before every send, check the email in:

  • Classic Outlook for Windows (Microsoft 365 desktop and older versions your audience uses)
  • New Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the web
  • Outlook for Mac, iOS and Android
  • Gmail, Apple Mail and Yahoo Mail, to make sure the Outlook fixes did not break anything else

Use an email testing tool that shows real screenshots, and send a live test to a real Outlook inbox for the final check. Our email testing checklist lists everything we check before a template ships.

Mini checklist before you hit send

  • Every layout block is a table with a width attribute.
  • Every image has a width attribute, display:block and alt text.
  • Buttons are table-cell or VML buttons, not padded links.
  • Background images have VML and a solid colour fallback.
  • Line heights include mso-line-height-rule: exactly.
  • The 96 DPI settings block and Office namespaces are present.
  • Conditional comments survived your ESP's editor.
  • The email was checked in classic Outlook, new Outlook and at least one browser-based client.

A Short Real-World Scenario

Here is a typical request. A Shopify brand designs a promo email in their ESP's drag-and-drop editor, then pastes in a custom hero block copied from their website. It looks great in Gmail. But in classic Outlook the hero image is missing, the button is a blue underlined link, and the product grid is one long column.

The fix follows the table above. The hero gets a VML background with a dark colour fallback. The button becomes a table-cell button. The product grid is rebuilt as a ghost table so two columns sit side by side in Outlook and stack on mobile. After a test pass in classic Outlook, new Outlook, Gmail and iOS Mail, the email goes out. If the same brand sends many campaigns, the better long-term move is a proper coded master template. That is what our custom HTML email template development service provides.

When to Rebuild Instead of Patch

If a template was built with a drag-and-drop builder or a web page framework, patching Outlook issues one by one often creates new ones in Gmail or mobile. In that case a clean rebuild is faster and cheaper over time. That is exactly what we did for Canadian Choice: their campaign template broke in Outlook, so we rebuilt it from scratch in 36 hours, and the campaign reached a 38% open rate.

If you are starting from a design file, our Figma to HTML email handoff checklist helps you avoid Outlook problems before any code is written.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my email look fine in Gmail but broken in Outlook?

Gmail uses a browser engine to display email, while classic Outlook for Windows uses Microsoft Word, which supports far less HTML and CSS. Code that relies on divs, margins, flexbox or background images works in Gmail but breaks in Outlook.

Does the new Outlook still need these fixes?

The new Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the web render email much like a browser, so they need fewer fixes. Many people still use classic Outlook, so a well-built email should work in both.

What is VML in HTML email?

VML (Vector Markup Language) is an old Microsoft format that classic Outlook still understands. Email developers use it inside MSO conditional comments to show rounded buttons and background images in Outlook.

Why does my Klaviyo or Mailchimp email break only in Outlook?

Builder blocks and custom code pasted into them are not always written for Word's engine, and some editors strip conditional comments. Check the sent HTML, not just the editor preview. Our post on why a Klaviyo email looks different in Outlook covers this in detail.

Short answer: a Klaviyo abandoned cart flow is an automated series of emails sent to shoppers who start checkout but do not buy. Build it on the Started Checkout metric, add a flow filter that stops it once the person places an order, send the first email within a few hours, and show the exact products they left behind with a dynamic block.

It is usually one of the highest-earning flows in any ecommerce store, because it reaches people who were seconds away from buying. Here is how to set it up properly. If you want it done for you, our Klaviyo flow setup service builds the full flow with branded templates.

Abandoned Cart vs Abandoned Checkout vs Browse Abandonment

  • Abandoned checkout: the shopper entered checkout (and usually their email) but did not pay. Triggered by Started Checkout. This is what most stores call the "abandoned cart flow".
  • Added to cart: the shopper added a product but never reached checkout. Needs an Added to Cart event, which Shopify stores send through the Klaviyo onsite tracking.
  • Browse abandonment: the shopper viewed products without adding them. Triggered by Viewed Product. Lower intent, softer emails.

Start with abandoned checkout. It has the highest intent and the clearest win. Once it runs well, add the other two as separate flows, and use filters so one shopper is not in all three at once.

Before You Build: Quick Checks

  • Your store integration is connected and Started Checkout events appear in Analytics > Metrics.
  • Onsite tracking is active if you plan an Added to Cart flow. On Shopify, check the Klaviyo app embed is turned on in your theme.
  • Your sending domain is set up. A branded sending domain with SPF, DKIM and DMARC helps flows reach the inbox; see how to set up DMARC for Klaviyo.
  • You have a welcome flow live too, since new subscribers and cart abandoners often overlap. Our Klaviyo welcome series guide covers that setup.

Step 1: Create the Flow and Choose the Trigger

  1. In Klaviyo, go to Flows and create a flow from scratch, or start from the abandoned cart template in the flow library.
  2. Choose a metric trigger and select Started Checkout from your store integration.
  3. Name it clearly, for example "Abandoned Checkout: 3 emails".

Step 2: Add Flow Filters So You Never Email Buyers

Filters are checked before every email, so they stop the flow the moment someone buys. Add:

  • Placed Order zero times since starting this flow. This is the most important filter.
  • Has not been in this flow in the last 7 to 14 days, so repeat visitors are not flooded with reminders.

Optionally add a trigger filter for cart value (for example, only carts above a minimum amount) if you plan to include discounts.

Step 3: Set the Timing

A proven starting point for three emails:

EmailDelayGoal
1. Reminder2 to 4 hours after checkout startedHelp them finish while the purchase is fresh
2. Reassurance24 hours laterAnswer doubts: reviews, delivery, returns
3. Last nudge48 to 72 hours laterFinal reminder, optional incentive

Test your own timing after a few weeks. Stores with expensive products often need longer gaps; fast-moving products can go quicker. Consider turning on smart sending carefully: it can skip a flow email if the person just received a campaign, which is usually fine, but check it does not skip the first reminder.

Step 4: Show the Cart With a Dynamic Product Block

The email should show exactly what they left behind: product image, name, variant, price and a button back to checkout. In Klaviyo's editor, use the Table or Product block with the event's line items, or the store's built-in abandoned cart block. Link the main button to the checkout URL from the event, so the cart is restored in one click.

In a custom HTML template, the same idea uses Klaviyo's template tags. A simplified loop looks like this:

{% for item in event.extra.line_items %}<tr><td><img src="{{ item.product.images.0.src }}" width="120" alt="{{ item.product.title }}"></td><td>{{ item.product.title }}<br>{{ item.line_price|floatformat:2 }}</td></tr>{% endfor %}

The exact property names depend on your store integration, so preview with a real event and adjust. The checkout button usually links to {{ event.extra.checkout_url }}.

Custom-coded templates make this block look on-brand in every inbox, including Outlook. Our custom Klaviyo email templates keep dynamic product areas editable in Klaviyo's drag-and-drop editor.

Step 5: Write the Three Emails

Email 1: A friendly reminder (no discount)

  • Subject line ideas: "You left something behind", "Still thinking it over?"
  • Show the cart, one short line of copy and a clear "Complete my order" button.
  • Keep it short. Most recoveries happen from this email.

Email 2: Remove the doubts

  • Add social proof: star ratings, one or two short reviews.
  • Answer common objections: delivery time, free returns, secure payment, support contact.

Email 3: The last nudge

  • Create gentle urgency: low stock or "your cart will expire soon", only if it is true.
  • If your margins allow, add a small incentive such as free shipping. Use a conditional split so only first-time buyers or high-value carts get it, which protects your margin.

Step 6: Add Smart Splits

  • New vs returning customers: returning customers rarely need a discount; new customers may need more reassurance.
  • Cart value: high-value carts can get a personal touch, such as a reply-to address for questions.

In Klaviyo, a split for new customers can use the condition "Placed Order zero times over all time". Keep splits few at first; each one doubles the emails you have to maintain.

Step 7: Test, Launch and Measure

  1. Preview each email with a real profile and event so the product block shows real items.
  2. Send tests to Gmail, Outlook and a phone, and check dark mode.
  3. Set the flow to Live.
  4. After two to four weeks, compare placed order rate and revenue per recipient for each email, and adjust timing, subject lines and incentives.

Our email testing checklist lists everything to check before you switch a flow to Live.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • No "Placed Order" filter, so buyers get "you forgot something" emails.
  • Giving a discount in the first email, which trains shoppers to abandon on purpose.
  • Generic emails without the actual products.
  • Templates that break in Outlook or on mobile. Read our guide on fixing emails that break in Outlook, and why a Klaviyo email looks different in Outlook.
  • Leaving the flow in Manual mode after testing, so emails queue but never send.

A Short Real-World Scenario

A Shopify store runs a single abandoned cart email with a generic "Come back!" message and a 10% code. Customers who already bought sometimes receive it, because there is no Placed Order filter. The rebuild adds the filter, splits the flow into three emails with the timing above, shows the real cart items, and moves the incentive to email 3 for first-time buyers only. The team then reviews revenue per recipient each month and tests one change at a time. Stores that also want theme or checkout changes can pair this with our Shopify development work.

Frequently Asked Questions

What trigger should I use for an abandoned cart flow in Klaviyo?

Use the Started Checkout metric for an abandoned checkout flow. If your store sends an Added to Cart event, you can build a separate, earlier flow for shoppers who add to cart but never reach checkout.

How many emails should an abandoned cart flow have?

Three emails is a strong starting point: a reminder after 2 to 4 hours, a reassurance email after about 24 hours, and a last nudge after 48 to 72 hours.

Should I offer a discount in abandoned cart emails?

Not in the first email. If you use one, put it in the last email and limit it with conditional splits, for example to first-time buyers or high-value carts.

Why is my abandoned cart flow not sending?

Check that the flow and each email are set to Live, that Started Checkout events are arriving, and that filters or smart sending are not excluding everyone.

Can I send SMS in the same flow?

Yes, Klaviyo lets you add SMS steps to a flow for subscribers who gave SMS consent. Keep SMS short and avoid sending it at the same time as an email.

Short answer: a Figma email design is ready for HTML when it is 600 to 640 pixels wide, built from simple stacked sections, uses web-safe fallback fonts, has a mobile version, marks every link and piece of live text, and comes with exported images and a dark mode check. Missing any of these usually means rework, delays and an email that looks different in Outlook.

We convert designs to code every day in our Figma to HTML email service. This is the checklist we wish every design file arrived with. It has 25 points grouped by topic, and you can hand it straight to your designer.

Why a Handoff Checklist Matters

Email is not a web page. Outlook for Windows uses Word to display email, Gmail strips some CSS, and phones stack everything into one column. A design that ignores these limits can still be coded, but the developer has to guess. Guesses lead to back-and-forth, and back-and-forth costs days. A clear file lets the developer code once and test once.

Layout and Size

  1. Frame width 600 to 640 px. Wider emails get cut off or shrunk in many inboxes.
  2. Stacked sections. Design in horizontal bands (header, hero, content blocks, footer). Each band becomes one table row in code.
  3. Two columns at most on desktop, three only for small items such as icons or products. Complex grids break in Outlook.
  4. Consistent spacing in multiples of 8 or 10 px, so padding can be coded exactly.
  5. No overlapping elements unless they are part of one flattened image. Email clients cannot position layers on top of each other reliably.

A useful habit: use Figma auto layout for each section. Auto layout maps closely to how tables and padding work in email code, so the developer can read spacing straight from the file.

Typography

  1. Name a fallback font for every custom font (for example Inter, then Arial). Outlook and many Android apps do not load web fonts.
  2. Body text 14 to 16 px, headlines 22 px or larger, line height about 1.4 to 1.6.
  3. Keep important text as live text, not inside images, so it shows when images are blocked, can be read by screen readers and helps deliverability.
  4. Use text styles in Figma so the developer can reuse the same sizes throughout the email.

In code, a font stack looks like font-family:'Inter', Arial, sans-serif;. Preview your design with the fallback font as well. If the headline wraps badly in Arial, adjust it now rather than after coding.

Images

  1. Export images at 2x the displayed size (for example 1200 px wide for a 600 px image) so they are sharp on retina screens.
  2. Keep file sizes small: under 200 KB per image where possible, and the whole email ideally under 1 MB.
  3. Flatten decorative effects (shadows, blurs, masks) into the image, because email clients do not support them in CSS.
  4. Write alt text for every image, or add it as a note next to each image in Figma.
  5. Avoid text over background images if you can. It needs special code for Outlook. If you use it, pick a solid fallback colour.

If a background image is essential to the design, the developer will use VML for Outlook. Our guide to Outlook background images with VML explains what that involves and why a fallback colour matters.

Buttons and Links

  1. Design buttons as simple rectangles with solid colours and live text. Gradients and complex shapes are harder to keep in Outlook.
  2. Buttons at least 44 px tall so they are easy to tap on phones.
  3. List every link: button URLs, image links, social icons, footer links and UTM parameters.
  4. Include the legal footer: company address, unsubscribe link and preference link.

Rounded corners are fine in most clients, but classic Outlook may show square corners unless the developer uses a VML button. See how bulletproof email buttons are built if your brand depends on a specific button shape.

Mobile and Dark Mode

  1. Add a mobile frame (about 375 px wide) showing how columns stack and which elements are hidden or resized.
  2. Check dark mode: avoid pure black text on transparent images and provide a light version of the logo if it is dark.
  3. Keep enough colour contrast for readability (aim for WCAG AA).

For dark mode, add a third frame on a dark grey background and drop in the logo and icons. Anything that disappears needs an outline or a light version. Our dark mode email design guide covers the details.

Platform Details

  1. Name the email platform (Klaviyo, Mailchimp, HubSpot and so on). The code is set up differently for each one's editor.
  2. Mark editable areas: which text, images and sections your team needs to change in the platform later.
  3. Mark dynamic content such as first name, product feeds or order details.
  4. Add preheader text, the short line shown after the subject in the inbox.

For example, a template for Klaviyo can be coded so each section is a drag-and-drop block your team can reorder, with product blocks linked to your catalogue. That is how we build custom Klaviyo email templates. Telling the developer the platform up front avoids rebuilding the template later.

How to Share the File

  • Share a Figma link with view access and Dev Mode (or export access) so images and measurements can be taken directly.
  • Put desktop and mobile frames side by side, clearly named.
  • Add a notes frame with links, fonts, platform and deadlines.

Mobile frameAbout 375 px, stacking shown
FontsFallback named for each custom font
ImagesExported at 2x, alt text noted
LinksEvery URL and UTM listed
PlatformNamed, editable areas marked
Dark modeLogo and icons checked on dark

Common Mistakes

  • Designing at 1440 px wide and scaling down, which makes text too small.
  • Only a desktop frame, leaving the developer to guess how the layout stacks.
  • Headlines set in a brand font with no fallback, which then look wrong in Outlook.
  • Links sent later in a separate chat, which delays delivery.
  • Components detached from the design system halfway through, so similar blocks have slightly different spacing.

A Short Real-World Scenario

A brand team designs a new collection launch email. The first file has one 1200 px desktop frame, a headline over a photo, and a custom font with no fallback. After a short review, the designer resizes to 600 px, adds a mobile frame, names Arial as the fallback, flattens the photo headline into live text on a solid block and lists all links in a notes frame. The developer can now code it in one pass. You can see a similar layout in our fashion new collection launch email.

Short answer: Gmail does not accept raw HTML code in its signature box. To add an HTML signature, open the signature in a web browser, select it, copy it, and paste it into Settings > See all settings > General > Signature. Images must be hosted online (not attached), and the signature must be under Gmail's 10,000-character limit.

If you do not have an HTML signature yet, our Gmail email signature service designs one that is built to paste into Gmail cleanly. If you already have one, the steps below take about five minutes.

Before You Start

  • Have your signature as an .html file or a web page link.
  • Make sure every image (logo, photo, icons) is hosted on a public URL, not embedded or attached. Gmail removes embedded images.
  • Use Gmail on a computer. The Gmail mobile apps only support plain text signatures.
  • Check which account you are in. If you use several Gmail or Google Workspace accounts, each one has its own signature settings.

How to check that images are hosted

Open the .html file in a text editor and look at each image tag. A hosted image looks like <img src="https://example.com/logo.png" width="120" alt="Company logo">. If the src starts with data:image, cid: or a local path such as C:\, the image will not survive in Gmail. Upload it to your website or another public host and update the link.

Step-by-Step: Add the Signature in Gmail

  1. Open the signature file in Chrome or another browser (double-click the .html file, or open the link you were given).
  2. Select the whole signature with your mouse, or press Ctrl+A (Windows) or Cmd+A (Mac).
  3. Copy it with Ctrl+C or Cmd+C.
  4. In Gmail, click the gear icon, then See all settings.
  5. On the General tab, scroll to Signature and click Create new. Give it a name.
  6. Paste the signature into the box with Ctrl+V or Cmd+V.
  7. Under Signature defaults, choose it for new emails and for replies and forwards.
  8. Scroll to the bottom and click Save Changes.
  9. Send a test email to yourself and to a colleague who uses Outlook, and check it on a phone.

Tip: if the file opens with a white page and lots of empty space, select only the signature area by dragging from the top-left corner of the signature to the bottom-right. Selecting the whole page sometimes copies extra blank lines.

Optional: turn off the dashes

Gmail can insert "--" above your signature. If you do not want it, find the option in the same Signature section to place the signature before quoted text and adjust how it appears in replies. The exact wording of these settings can change, so look for it near the signature defaults.

Fixing Common Gmail Signature Problems

Images do not show

The images are probably embedded or attached. Host them online (your website, or a storage service with public links) and make sure the signature's HTML points to those URLs. If the links are correct but images still do not load for some recipients, their email client may block images by default. Our guide on why email images are not showing covers the other causes.

"Signature is too long" error

Gmail limits signatures to 10,000 characters of code. Remove unused styles, shorten tracking links, and avoid copying extra page content. A well-coded signature is far under the limit.

The layout changes or spacing collapses

Gmail strips some CSS. Signatures should be built with tables and inline styles, which Gmail keeps. If yours was made in a word processor, it will not paste reliably.

Images look blurry

Use images exported at twice their displayed size and set a fixed width in the HTML, so they look sharp on retina screens.

The signature looks different in Outlook

Your recipients' email client renders the signature, not Gmail. A signature built only for Gmail can break in Outlook. See our guide on adding an HTML signature in Outlook and how cross-client HTML signatures are built.

Icons or logo vanish in dark mode

Dark logos and black social icons can disappear when the recipient uses dark mode. Use icons with a light outline or a coloured background. Our dark mode email design guide explains the options.

What a Gmail-Safe Signature Looks Like in Code

A reliable signature uses a simple table, inline styles and hosted images with fixed widths. A trimmed example:

<table cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0"><tr><td style="padding-right:12px;"><img src="https://example.com/photo.png" width="80" alt="Jane Doe"></td><td style="font:14px/20px Arial,sans-serif;color:#333333;"><strong>Jane Doe</strong><br>Head of Sales</td></tr></table>

No external stylesheet, no div-based layout, no background images and no web fonts. Those are the features Gmail and Outlook handle poorly in signatures.

Common Mistakes

  • Pasting the HTML code itself into the signature box, which shows the code as text.
  • Using a signature image (one big picture of the whole signature). It looks blank when images are off and the text cannot be clicked.
  • Forgetting to set the default for replies, so replies go out without a signature.
  • Linking images from a private folder, such as a Google Drive file that needs a login.
  • Adding too many social icons and banners, which pushes the signature past the character limit.

Rolling Out Signatures for a Google Workspace Team

For a team, installing signatures one by one gets messy. Options:

  • Admin console: Google Workspace admins can add a simple footer for all outgoing mail under Apps > Google Workspace > Gmail > Compliance > Append footer. It is appended below each email, separately from personal signatures.
  • Per-person installs: give each person their personal signature file and a one-page guide, like the steps above.
  • Signature tools: dedicated signature management tools can push signatures to everyone automatically.

We designed one consistent signature for Apex Financial's 50+ person team, with an installation guide so every employee could set it up in minutes.

A short real-world scenario

A ten-person agency moves to Google Workspace. Each person copies an old signature from Outlook, and the results look different: some have the logo, some have broken images, and one has the logo at full size. The fix is one master design, coded once, with a personal .html file per team member and images hosted on the company website. Each person follows the nine steps above, and a manager checks one test email from everyone. You can see a finished example in our professional HTML email signature project.

No. Gmail's signature box does not accept code. Open the HTML signature in a browser, copy the rendered signature, and paste it into Gmail.

Gmail removes embedded and attached images. Host each image online and make sure the signature points to those public image URLs.

The Gmail app only supports plain text signatures. If no mobile signature is set, it can use your desktop signature depending on your settings, so always check how emails sent from your phone look.

Yes. Create two signatures in the Signature section and choose one for new emails and a shorter one for replies and forwards under Signature defaults.

Short answer: in the new Outlook and Outlook on the web, go to Settings > Accounts > Signatures, paste the signature you copied from a browser, and save. In classic Outlook for Windows, go to File > Options > Mail > Signatures, or copy the signature's .htm file into the Signatures folder for a pixel-perfect result. Each Outlook app keeps its own signature, so set it up in every version you use.

Need a signature that works everywhere? Our Outlook email signature service builds signatures for classic and new Outlook, Mac and mobile. If you already have a signature file, follow the steps for your version below.

Before You Start

  • Have the signature as an .html or .htm file, with all images hosted online.
  • Know which Outlook you use: new Outlook for Windows, classic Outlook for Windows, Outlook on the web (outlook.com or Microsoft 365 in a browser), or Outlook for Mac.
  • Back up any existing signature you want to keep. Replacing files in the Signatures folder overwrites them.

How to tell which Outlook you have

If you seeYou are using
A File tab at the top leftClassic Outlook for Windows
A "New Outlook" toggle and a gear icon, no File tabNew Outlook for Windows
Outlook open in a browser tabOutlook on the web
An Outlook menu in the Mac menu barOutlook for Mac

Menu names can change between updates, so if a label looks slightly different, look for the closest match. The two Windows apps render email differently, which is explained in new Outlook vs classic Outlook rendering.

New Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the Web

  1. Open the signature file in a web browser, select it all and copy it.
  2. In Outlook, open Settings (gear icon) > Accounts > Signatures.
  3. Click New signature, name it and paste the signature into the box.
  4. Choose it as the default for new messages and for replies and forwards.
  5. Click Save and send yourself a test email.

In Microsoft 365, signatures set in Outlook on the web and the new Outlook can sync between the two when roaming signatures are turned on for your account.

Classic Outlook for Windows

Method 1: Copy and paste

  1. Open the signature in a browser, select it all and copy it.
  2. In Outlook, go to File > Options > Mail > Signatures.
  3. Click New, name the signature and paste it into the editing box.
  4. Choose the default signature for new messages and replies, then click OK.

Pasting works for simple signatures, but Outlook's Word editor can change spacing and image sizes.

Method 2: Install the .htm file (most accurate)

  1. Create a signature in Outlook with any placeholder text and give it a name, for example "Company". Close Outlook.
  2. Press Windows + R, type %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Signatures and press Enter.
  3. Replace the file Company.htm with your signature file, keeping exactly the same name.
  4. Open Outlook again and select the signature as your default.

This keeps the original code, so the signature looks exactly as designed.

A tip for Method 2: do not open and re-save the signature in Outlook's editor afterwards. Editing it there rewrites the .htm file with Word's own markup, and you lose the clean code. If you need to change something, edit the file and replace it again.

Outlook for Mac

  1. Open the signature in Safari or Chrome, select it and copy it.
  2. In Outlook, go to Outlook > Settings > Signatures.
  3. Click + to add a signature, paste it, name it and close the window to save.
  4. Set the default signature for each account under Default signatures.

Outlook for iPhone and Android

The Outlook mobile apps support a simpler signature, set under Settings > Signature. Keep it to your name, role and phone number, or ask for a mobile-friendly version of your signature.

What an Outlook-Safe Signature Looks Like

Classic Outlook ignores many modern CSS features. A signature that survives uses tables for layout, inline styles and fixed image widths set as attributes, not only in CSS:

<img src="https://example.com/logo.png" width="140" height="40" alt="Company" style="display:block;border:0;">

Avoid div layouts, background images, web fonts and margins. Use padding on table cells instead. This is how our HTML email signature designs are coded, so the same file works in Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail.

Fixing Common Outlook Signature Problems

Images show as attachments or red crosses

Images must be hosted online and linked in the HTML. Embedded images often turn into attachments. Hosted images display as long as the recipient allows images.

Spacing is too big or the layout breaks

Classic Outlook uses Word to display email, so signatures must be built with tables, inline styles and fixed image widths. Read why emails break in Outlook to understand the cause.

Images look huge or blurry

Set a fixed width attribute on each image in the HTML, and use images exported at twice the displayed size.

The signature is different on each device

Each Outlook app stores its own signature. Install it in every app you use, or use Microsoft 365 roaming signatures between Outlook on the web and the new Outlook.

The logo disappears for some recipients

Recipients using dark mode may not see a dark logo on a transparent background. Add a light outline or a solid background behind the logo. Our dark mode email design guide shows how.

Common Mistakes

  • Setting up the signature in one Outlook app and assuming it appears in the others.
  • Replacing the .htm file while Outlook is still open, so the change does not load.
  • Renaming the file, so Outlook no longer finds it.
  • Using a single large image as the whole signature, which shows as blank or as an attachment.
  • Forgetting to set the default for replies and forwards.

Rolling Out Signatures Across a Company

For teams on Microsoft 365, admins can add organisation-wide disclaimers with Exchange mail flow rules, or use a signature management tool. For smaller teams, a standard signature file per person and a simple install guide work well. That is how we delivered one consistent signature for Apex Financial's 50+ person team. Using Gmail too? See how to add an HTML signature in Gmail, or our Gmail email signature service.

A short real-world scenario

An office manager pastes the new company signature into classic Outlook. The logo doubles in size and the lines have large gaps. Switching to Method 2, the manager creates a placeholder called "Company", closes Outlook, drops in the supplied Company.htm and reopens Outlook. The signature now matches the design. The same file, copied from a browser, is then pasted into new Outlook on two laptops. A test email from each app confirms they match. They store signatures separately and render them differently. The new Outlook uses a browser engine, while classic Outlook uses Word. A signature built with tables and inline styles looks the same in both.

Short answer: Gmail clips any email whose HTML code is larger than about 102 KB. Everything after that point is hidden behind a "[Message clipped] View entire message" link, which often hides your footer, unsubscribe link and tracking pixel. Images do not count, because they are hosted separately. The fix is to make the HTML itself smaller: remove unused code, repeated inline styles and heavy builder markup.

We see this problem constantly in templates made with drag-and-drop builders. It is one of the first things we check in our email testing and QA service. This guide explains what the limit is, what counts toward it, how to measure your email and how to bring the size down without changing the design.

Why Gmail Clipping Hurts Your Results

  • Hidden content: offers, products and calls to action below the cut are never seen by most readers. Few people click "View entire message".
  • Missing unsubscribe link: readers who cannot find it may mark you as spam instead, which damages deliverability.
  • Broken open tracking: the tracking pixel usually sits at the bottom, so clipped emails can under-report opens.
  • Legal footer out of sight: your company address and preference links sit in the footer, which is exactly the part that gets cut.

The worst part is that clipping is silent. Your email platform reports a normal send, and nothing warns you. You only find out if you open a real test in Gmail and scroll to the end.

What Counts Toward the 102 KB Limit

Only the HTML file size counts: tags, inline styles, comments, whitespace, hidden text and any code your email platform adds. Hosted images, fonts loaded from a URL and linked files do not count. Remember that your email platform (Klaviyo, Mailchimp, HubSpot) adds its own tracking and wrapper code when it sends, so aim for 80 to 90 KB of HTML to leave a safety margin.

Counts toward the limitDoes not count
HTML tags and attributesImages hosted on a server
Inline style attributesWeb fonts loaded from a URL
CSS in the <style> blockLanding pages you link to
Comments, spaces and line breaksAttachments (not used in marketing email)
Hidden sections and preheader padding
Tracking links your platform rewrites

Special characters matter too. Characters such as emoji or accented letters can take more than one byte each, and some platforms convert them to longer entity codes. This is rarely the main problem, but it adds up in long emails.

How to Check Your Email's Size

  1. Export or copy the final HTML from your email platform (the version it actually sends).
  2. Save it as a .html file and check the file size, or paste it into an HTML size checker.
  3. Send a real test to a Gmail inbox and scroll to the bottom. If you see "[Message clipped]", you are over the limit.

A quick way to see the size from a terminal is to save the file and run a byte count, for example wc -c email.html on Mac or Linux. The number is in bytes, so 102,000 bytes is roughly the limit. Always measure the sent version, not the file from your code editor, because the platform adds code on the way out.

8 Ways to Stay Under the Limit

  1. Minify the HTML before sending: remove line breaks, indentation and comments. This alone often saves 10 to 20%.
  2. Remove repeated inline styles. Builders repeat the same long style attribute on every element. Put shared styles in the head for clients that support them and keep inline styles short.
  3. Delete unused sections that are hidden with display:none. Hidden code still counts.
  4. Avoid pasting from Word or Google Docs, which adds large amounts of invisible markup.
  5. Keep Outlook fixes lean. MSO conditional code and VML are necessary, but only where they are needed.
  6. Use fewer, simpler tables. Deeply nested tables multiply code size quickly.
  7. Shorten long tracking links or use your platform's link tracking instead of adding many parameters by hand.
  8. Split very long emails into a shorter email plus a link to a landing page or blog post.

Example: trimming a repeated style

A builder might output this on every paragraph:

<td style="font-family:Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size:16px; line-height:24px; color:#333333; mso-line-height-rule:exactly; text-align:left; padding:0px 0px 0px 0px;">

A hand-coded version keeps only what the element needs and drops zero values:

<td style="font:16px/24px Arial,sans-serif;color:#333333;">

Across 60 or 80 cells, that difference is several kilobytes. Test shorthand in Outlook before relying on it everywhere, and keep the longer form where a client needs it.

Example: Outlook code only where needed

Wrap Outlook-only code in a conditional comment, such as <!--[if mso]> ... <![endif]-->, and use it once per section, not once per element. If you use background images, our guide to Outlook background images with VML shows a compact pattern.

Common Mistakes

  • Measuring the wrong file. The editor preview is smaller than what the platform sends.
  • Hiding a desktop and a mobile version of the same block. Both versions are in the code, so the size doubles.
  • Stacking product grids. Long product feeds with many columns grow fast. Show fewer items and link to the collection.
  • Leaving old sections in saved templates. Each campaign copied from the last one can carry dead code forward.
  • Base64 images. Images embedded as data in the HTML count toward the limit and can push an email over by themselves.

Builder Templates vs Hand-Coded Templates

A drag-and-drop template often reaches 120 to 200 KB because of wrapper code and repeated styles. A hand-coded template with the same design is usually 40 to 70 KB. That is why our custom HTML email templates are built lean from the start, and why they stay editable in Klaviyo and Mailchimp without growing out of control. If you already have a coded template, see how to use a custom HTML template in Klaviyo so the platform does not add extra wrappers.

A Short Real-World Scenario

A store sends a weekly newsletter with a hero, three editorial blocks and a twelve-product grid. The email looks fine in the builder. In Gmail, the last four products and the whole footer vanish behind "[Message clipped]". Checking the sent HTML shows it is well over the limit, mostly from repeated styles and a hidden mobile copy of the product grid. The fix is to rebuild the grid once with responsive stacking, trim the styles and cut the grid to eight products with a "Shop all" button. The email drops comfortably under 90 KB, and the footer is visible again. Long, content-heavy sends like this are where lean newsletter email templates pay off.

Mini Checklist Before Every Send

  • Sent HTML is under 90 KB.
  • No base64 images and no hidden duplicate blocks.
  • Comments and whitespace removed.
  • Test opened in Gmail web and the Gmail app, scrolled to the end.
  • Unsubscribe link and address visible without clicking "View entire message".

Clipping is only one of the checks every email should pass. See our 25-point email testing checklist, and if your layout also breaks in Outlook, read how to fix HTML emails that break in Outlook.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Gmail's email size limit?

Gmail clips messages when the HTML code exceeds about 102 KB. The rest of the message is hidden behind a "View entire message" link.

Do images count toward Gmail clipping?

No. Images hosted on a server are loaded separately and do not count. Only the HTML code, including inline styles and hidden content, counts. Images embedded as base64 data inside the HTML do count.

How do I stop Gmail from clipping my emails?

Reduce the HTML size: minify the code, remove repeated inline styles and hidden sections, and simplify nested tables. Aim for 80 to 90 KB to leave room for code your email platform adds.

Does clipping affect deliverability?

Indirectly, yes. If readers cannot find the unsubscribe link, some will click "Report spam" instead, and spam complaints hurt your sender reputation over time.

Does the Gmail app clip emails too?

Yes. Clipping applies in Gmail on the web and in the Gmail mobile apps, so check both when you test.

Short answer: a Klaviyo welcome series is an automated flow that greets new subscribers. Trigger it when someone joins your newsletter list, send the first email right away, then follow with 3 or 4 more emails over about 10 days that introduce your brand, show best sellers, share reviews and give a reason to place the first order. Stop the flow for anyone who buys.

New subscribers are at their most interested in the first few days. A good welcome series turns that interest into a first purchase. If you want it built for you, our Klaviyo flow setup service handles the flow, the logic and the templates.

Once it is live, a welcome series runs every day without any extra work. That makes it one of the first flows most stores set up, together with abandoned cart. The steps below walk through the trigger, the filters, the five emails and the small settings that often get missed.

Step 1: Choose the Trigger

  • In Klaviyo, go to Flows and create a flow (or start from the welcome series template).
  • Choose a list trigger: "When someone is added to this list" and select your newsletter list. Your signup forms should add people to that list.
  • If you run a discount pop-up, use the list that form feeds so the discount email matches the promise.

Check that every signup form on your site points to the same list, including the footer form, the pop-up and any checkout opt-in you sync from Shopify. A form that feeds a different list means those subscribers never get the welcome series. If you see many strange sign-ups, add protection first; see how to stop fake sign-ups in Klaviyo, because bots entering a welcome flow will bounce and hurt your sender reputation.

Step 2: Add Flow Filters

  • Placed Order zero times since starting this flow, so buyers stop receiving "please buy" emails.
  • Optionally, has not placed an order ever for emails with a first-order discount, so existing customers are not offered one.

Flow filters are checked before every email, so a subscriber who buys on day 3 will not get the day 6 offer. This is the single most important setting in the flow. Without it, new customers keep receiving discount emails after paying full price, which leads to complaints and refund requests.

Step 3: The 5 Emails and When to Send Them

EmailTimingGoal
1. Welcome and brand storyRight awaySay thanks, deliver any promised discount, set expectations
2. Best sellersDay 2Show the products most people buy first
3. Reviews and proofDay 4Build trust with customer reviews and photos
4. First-order offer or reason to buyDay 6Make the first purchase easy: offer, free shipping or guarantee
5. Last reminderDay 9Remind them the offer is ending, point to help and returns

In the flow builder, add a time delay between each email. For example: email 1, wait 2 days, email 2, wait 2 days, email 3, and so on. You can also set smart sending off for the first email so a new subscriber gets it even if they received a campaign recently.

What to Put in Each Email

Email 1: Welcome

Keep it warm and short: a thank you, one sentence about why your brand exists, the discount code if you promised one, and a single clear button. This email usually has the highest open rate of anything you send.

If you use unique coupon codes, Klaviyo adds them with a tag like this in the email body:

{% coupon_code 'WELCOME10' %}

Replace WELCOME10 with the name of the coupon you set up in Klaviyo. Unique codes stop one code being shared across coupon sites.

Email 2: Best sellers

Use a product grid of 3 to 6 best sellers. A dynamic product block keeps it up to date automatically. Our custom Klaviyo email templates keep these blocks editable in Klaviyo's editor.

Email 3: Reviews

Show two or three short reviews with star ratings and real customer photos if you have them. Use real reviews only, and keep them short enough to read on a phone.

Email 4: The offer

Give a clear reason to buy now. If you do not want to discount, offer free shipping, a gift or a guarantee instead.

Email 5: Last reminder

Short reminder that the offer ends soon, plus links to shipping, returns and support.

Common Welcome Series Mistakes

  • No purchase filter. Buyers keep getting "buy now" emails.
  • Discount not delivered. The pop-up promises 10% off but email 1 does not show a code.
  • Too many links. Email 1 with ten links and three buttons splits attention. One main action works better.
  • Flow left in draft or manual mode. Each email must be set to Live, not only the flow.
  • Judging success by opens alone. Apple Mail Privacy Protection can inflate opens. Watch clicks and placed orders instead; see open rates and Apple Mail privacy.
  • Broken layout in Outlook. Drag-and-drop blocks mixed with pasted code often break. A clean custom HTML template in Klaviyo avoids this.

Tips That Improve Results

  • Use a conditional split for people who joined through a discount form versus a footer signup.
  • Keep the design consistent with your campaigns so subscribers recognise you.
  • Test every email in Gmail, Outlook and on mobile. See our email testing checklist.
  • After the welcome series, a strong abandoned cart flow catches shoppers who start checkout but do not finish.
  • If your sending domain is new, launch the flow gradually and follow a sending domain warm-up plan.

For a real example of what a redesigned flow can do, read how TechFlow raised onboarding completion by 121%, or see our welcome email design.

Launch Checklist

  1. All signup forms add people to the trigger list.
  2. Flow filter "Placed Order zero times since starting this flow" is set.
  3. Time delays match the plan.
  4. Coupon codes show correctly in a test send.
  5. Each email is tested on mobile, Gmail and Outlook.
  6. Every email is switched to Live.
  7. You have signed up with a fresh address to see the real experience.

A Real-World Scenario

A small homeware store has a pop-up offering 10% off, but the pop-up feeds a list that no flow uses. New subscribers get nothing until the next weekly campaign, and many forget why they signed up. The store connects the pop-up list to a five-email welcome series, adds the purchase filter and uses a unique coupon in email 1. They also point the footer form to the same list and use a conditional split so footer sign-ups get a free shipping message instead of a code. Now every new subscriber hears from the brand within minutes, and buyers leave the flow as soon as they order.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many emails should a Klaviyo welcome series have?

Three to five emails over about 7 to 10 days works well for most stores. Start with three and add more once you see how subscribers respond.

What trigger should I use for a welcome series in Klaviyo?

Use a list trigger for your newsletter list, so everyone added through your signup forms enters the flow.

Should the welcome series include a discount?

Only if you promised one at signup or your margins allow it. Free shipping, a gift or a guarantee can work as well as a discount.

Will existing subscribers get the welcome series when I turn it on?

No. A list-triggered flow only includes people added after it goes live, unless you choose to add past subscribers when you set it up. Most stores leave existing subscribers out.

How do I know if my welcome series is working?

Look at clicks, placed orders and revenue per recipient in the flow analytics, not only open rates. Compare each email to see where people drop off, then test changes one at a time.

Short answer: in dark mode, some email clients leave your email alone, some darken only light backgrounds, and some invert almost every colour. You cannot fully control that, but you can design for it: use transparent logos with an outline or light version, avoid pure black and pure white, add dark mode styles for clients that support them, and test in each client before sending.

Many readers now keep their phones and computers in dark mode all day, so your email is often seen that way first. This guide covers how clients behave, the problems you will see, and the design and code fixes that make an email hold up.

The Three Ways Email Clients Handle Dark Mode

BehaviourWhat happensWhere you see it
No changeThe email keeps its colours; only the app interface turns darkSome webmail and desktop clients
Partial inversionLight backgrounds become dark and dark text becomes light; dark areas stayFor example Gmail on Android and Outlook.com
Full inversionMost colours are inverted, including dark areasFor example Outlook apps and Gmail on iOS

Behaviour changes as email apps update, so always check the current result in real clients rather than relying on a fixed list. There is also a fourth case worth knowing: clients such as Apple Mail respect your own dark mode styles if you provide them, which gives you the most control.

Common Dark Mode Problems

  • A dark logo on a transparent background disappears on a dark background.
  • Brand colours shift to a different shade after inversion.
  • Text inside images stays dark while the background around it turns dark.
  • Buttons lose contrast, or borders appear where there were none.
  • Product photos cut out on white look like floating white boxes on a dark page.
  • Dividers and thin grey lines vanish or turn into bright stripes.

Design Fixes

  1. Logos: use a transparent PNG with a thin light outline or glow, or supply a light version to swap in with dark mode styles.
  2. Avoid pure black (#000) and pure white (#fff) for large areas. Slightly off-white and off-black invert more gracefully.
  3. Keep text as live text, not inside images, so the client can recolour it.
  4. Give images a built-in background or padding so they do not look cut out on dark backgrounds.
  5. Check button contrast in both modes; a solid brand-coloured button with white text usually survives.

Buttons deserve special care. A coded button with live text and a background colour set on the table cell holds up better than an image button. Our guide to bulletproof email buttons shows the pattern that works in Outlook as well.

Design in both modes from the start

If your team designs in Figma, add a dark mode frame next to the light one. Place your logo, icons and key images on a dark grey background and see what disappears. This takes minutes at the design stage and saves a round of fixes after coding.

Code Fixes

  • Declare support in the head: <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> and <meta name="supported-color-schemes" content="light dark">.
  • Add styles inside @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) for clients that support it, such as Apple Mail and iOS Mail, to set your own dark colours and swap logos.
  • For Outlook.com and the Outlook apps, dark mode attribute selectors (such as [data-ogsc]) can target text colours in some versions.
  • Keep all key colours set inline as well, so clients that ignore the head styles still show a sensible result.

Example: a simple dark mode block

In the <style> block, add classes for dark mode and apply them to your elements:

@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { .dm-bg { background-color:#1e1e1e !important; } .dm-text { color:#f2f2f2 !important; } .logo-light { display:block !important; } .logo-dark { display:none !important; } }

Then give the body table class="dm-bg", text cells class="dm-text", and include two logo images: the normal one with class="logo-dark" and a light one hidden by default with class="logo-light" and style="display:none;". Clients that do not support the media query simply show the normal logo. Keep the hidden logo small, since hidden code still adds to the email's size.

Common Mistakes

  • Relying only on the media query. Gmail and the Outlook apps ignore it, so the email must still look acceptable without it.
  • Using a black logo with no outline. It is the number one cause of "missing logo" complaints.
  • Putting headlines inside images. They cannot be recoloured, and they also fail when images are blocked.
  • Testing only on your own phone. Your phone shows one client's behaviour, not your audience's.
  • Chasing perfect control. Aim for readable and on-brand in every client, not identical.

Test Before Every Send

Dark mode is where emails most often surprise people. Preview every email in dark mode in Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail, on desktop and mobile. It is part of our 25-point email testing checklist, and dark mode repairs are included in our Outlook and email rendering fix service. Outlook has its own quirks too; see how to fix emails that break in Outlook, and note that the new and classic Outlook apps can differ, as explained in new Outlook vs classic Outlook rendering.

For an example, our Black Friday email uses locked dark mode colours so the design stays on-brand in every client. Every custom HTML email template we build is checked in light and dark mode before delivery, including templates we build for Klaviyo.

Mini dark mode checklist

  • Logo readable on dark grey and on white.
  • All headlines and body copy are live text.
  • Buttons have enough contrast in both modes.
  • Product images have a background or padding.
  • Colour-scheme meta tags are in the head.
  • Tested in Gmail (Android and iOS), Outlook and Apple Mail in dark mode.

Why Your Logo Disappears in Dark Mode

This is the most common dark mode complaint. A black or dark-coloured logo saved as a transparent PNG sits on a white background in light mode. When the client turns that background dark, the logo blends in and seems to vanish. Three fixes work well:

  • Add a thin white outline or soft glow around the logo in the PNG. It is invisible on white and keeps the logo readable on dark.
  • Place the logo on a solid light shape such as a rounded white badge, so the colours behind it never change.
  • Swap in a light logo with @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) for Apple Mail and iOS Mail, and keep the outline version as the default for other clients.

A Short Real-World Scenario

A fashion brand launches a new collection with a navy logo, black headline text in an image and a white product grid. In light mode it looks clean. In dark mode on an iPhone, the logo disappears, the headline image shows as a white rectangle, and the product photos float on bright squares. The fix: an outlined logo plus a light version for Apple Mail, the headline rebuilt as live text, and product photos placed on a soft grey background inside the image. The next send is readable in every client tested, even though each client still shows slightly different colours. Good contrast also helps readers with low vision; see our accessible email design guide.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I stop email clients from changing my colours in dark mode?

Not completely. Some clients invert colours regardless of your code. You can reduce the impact with careful colour choices, dark mode styles for supporting clients and testing.

Why does my logo disappear in dark mode?

A dark logo on a transparent background blends into a dark background. Add a light outline or glow, or swap in a light logo using dark mode styles.

Does Outlook support dark mode styles?

Support varies by version. Outlook apps and Outlook.com often apply their own inversion, so test the specific versions your audience uses.

Does Gmail support prefers-color-scheme?

At the time of writing, Gmail generally ignores the prefers-color-scheme media query and applies its own colour changes, so design choices matter most there.

Should I design a fully dark email instead?

You can, but some clients will invert it to light. A dark design still needs testing in both modes, just like a light one.

Yes. We fix dark mode issues in existing templates and build new templates that are checked in light and dark mode. See pricing or request a free quote.

Short answer: before sending any email, check that it renders correctly in Outlook, Gmail, Apple Mail and on mobile; that it stays under Gmail's 102 KB limit; that it looks right in dark mode; that every link, merge tag and image works; that it is readable and accessible; and that your platform settings (subject, preheader, audience, unsubscribe) are correct.

This is the same checklist we use for every email in our email testing and QA service. Copy it into your own pre-send routine.

Once an email is sent, you cannot take it back. A broken button, a wrong price or a layout that falls apart in Outlook reaches every subscriber at once. A short, repeatable checklist catches most of these problems in minutes. The 25 points below are grouped so you can work through them in order, from how the email looks to how it is sent.

Rendering (1–6)

  1. Classic Outlook for Windows shows the layout correctly (columns, spacing, buttons).
  2. New Outlook and Outlook on the web look the same.
  3. Gmail on web, Android and iOS shows the full design.
  4. Apple Mail and iOS Mail render correctly.
  5. Yahoo Mail and other clients your audience uses are checked.
  6. Web fonts fall back to a clean system font where unsupported.

Classic Outlook for Windows uses Microsoft Word to render HTML, which is why it breaks layouts other clients handle well. New Outlook uses a more modern engine, so the two can look quite different. See new Outlook vs classic Outlook rendering for what changes between them.

For font fallback, always list a safe system font after your web font:

font-family: 'Inter', Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;

Mobile (7–9)

  1. Columns stack neatly on a phone.
  2. Text is at least 14 px and buttons at least 44 px tall.
  3. Images scale down without stretching or cropping key content.

Most people read email on a phone, so mobile checks matter as much as desktop ones. Open the test on a real phone, not only a resized browser window. If columns refuse to stack, our guide on responsive email not working on mobile covers the usual causes, such as missing media queries or fixed widths.

Size and Dark Mode (10–12)

  1. The HTML is under 102 KB, so Gmail does not clip it. See how to fix Gmail clipping.
  2. The email looks right in dark mode in Gmail, Outlook and Apple Mail. See our dark mode email design guide.
  3. Logos and icons stay visible on dark backgrounds.

A quick way to check size is to save the final HTML as a file and look at its size on disk. Remember that your platform may add tracking code when it sends, so aim to stay well under the limit, not just under it. For dark mode, a dark logo on a transparent PNG is the most common problem; a thin light outline or a light background behind the logo usually fixes it.

Links and Content (13–18)

  1. Every link and button goes to the right page.
  2. UTM or tracking parameters are correct and consistent.
  3. Merge tags such as first name show real values, with a fallback if empty.
  4. Dynamic product or order blocks show the right items.
  5. Prices, dates, codes and offer terms are correct.
  6. Spelling and grammar are checked.

Merge tags need a default so an empty field does not leave an awkward gap. In Klaviyo, for example, a first name with a fallback looks like this:

{{ first_name|default:'there' }}

Click every link in the real test email, not in the editor preview. Tracking wrappers are added at send time, and that is where broken links often show up. Buttons should be built from code so they still work when images are off; see bulletproof email buttons.

Images and Accessibility (19–22)

  1. Every image has meaningful alt text; decorative images have empty alt.
  2. The email still makes sense with images turned off.
  3. Text and button colours have enough contrast.
  4. Important text is live text, not only inside images.

A decorative image should use an empty alt attribute, like alt="", so screen readers skip it. A content image needs alt text that says what it shows or what it offers. For more on screen readers, heading order and contrast, read our accessible email design guide.

Platform and Deliverability (23–25)

  1. Subject line and preheader text are set and fit on mobile.
  2. The right list or segment is selected, and send time and time zone are correct.
  3. The unsubscribe link and company address are in the footer and work.

These last three checks are easy to skip because they live in the platform settings, not the design. They also cause some of the most visible mistakes, such as sending a VIP offer to the whole list or sending at 3 a.m. in your main market.

Common Testing Mistakes

  • Testing only in the editor preview. Previews are not real email clients. Always send real tests.
  • Checking one Outlook version. Classic Outlook, new Outlook and Outlook on the web behave differently.
  • Skipping images-off. Many work inboxes block images by default.
  • Retesting nothing after a small change. A last-minute text edit can push a file over the size limit or break a table.
  • One person doing everything. A second pair of eyes catches wrong prices and dates much more often.

Make Testing Faster

  • Use an email testing tool that shows screenshots across clients, then send a final real test to Gmail and Outlook.
  • Start from a well-built template: most rendering problems come from the template, not the content. Our hand-coded email templates are tested in 50+ clients before delivery.
  • If you are handing designs to a developer, the Figma to HTML handoff checklist prevents problems before coding starts.

See what testing and a clean rebuild did for Canadian Choice: their campaign email now renders correctly in every Outlook version.

A Real-World Scenario

A marketing manager is about to send a spring sale. The design looks great in the editor. She runs the checklist and finds three problems: the hero headline is baked into an image with no alt text, the discount code in the footer still shows last month's code, and the two-column product grid does not stack on her phone. Fixing all three takes twenty minutes. Without the check, every subscriber would have seen a wrong code, and phone readers would have seen tiny, squeezed products.

Which email clients should I test in?

At minimum: classic Outlook for Windows, Gmail (web and mobile), Apple Mail and iOS Mail. Then add the clients your own audience uses most, which you can see in your email platform's reports.

How do I test an email in Outlook without Windows?

Use an email testing tool that renders screenshots in real Outlook versions, or send a test to a colleague who uses classic Outlook for Windows.

Yes, but it is faster. The layout is already proven, so focus on links, content, images, merge tags and platform settings. Do a full rendering check after any template change.

Is a testing tool enough on its own?

It is a big help, but also send a real test to Gmail and Outlook and open it on a phone. Real inboxes show tracking links, images-off views and dark mode more reliably.

Short answer: white-label email development means a specialist team builds HTML emails, templates and Klaviyo flows for your agency's clients, and you deliver the work under your own brand. The client never deals with the partner. It lets agencies take on more email work, offer email as a new service and keep their margins, without hiring and training email developers.

Many web, design and marketing agencies get asked for email work sooner or later. A client wants a new newsletter template, a Klaviyo welcome flow or a fix for emails that break in Outlook. Saying no sends that client to another agency. Saying yes without the right skills can lead to broken emails and unhappy clients. A white-label partner sits in the middle: you keep the client relationship, and the partner does the specialist build quietly in the background.

Why Agencies Use a White-Label Email Partner

  • Email is specialist work. Coding emails that work in Outlook, Gmail and dark mode is very different from building websites. Email still relies on tables, inline styles and fallbacks for old rendering engines. A strong web developer can lose days learning these rules.
  • Demand is uneven. Some months you have ten email projects, some months none. A partner scales with you, so you are not paying a full-time salary during quiet months.
  • Faster delivery. A specialist team codes and tests an email in 24 to 48 hours, because they have done the same work many times and have a tested base of code to start from.
  • New revenue. You can sell email templates, Klaviyo flows and campaign builds without building a team first. Email becomes a line on your service menu instead of a request you turn down.
  • Less risk. A broken email goes to thousands of people at once. Handing the build to a team that tests every send lowers the chance of a public mistake with your client's brand.

How the Process Works

  1. You sell the project and agree the brief with your client.
  2. You send the design (Figma, PSD or XD) or brief to the partner, with the platform and deadline.
  3. The partner builds and tests the email in 50+ clients and returns files or uploads to the client's platform under your account.
  4. You review, present it to your client as your own work and handle feedback.
  5. Revisions go back to the partner and return quickly.

The key point is that you stay the single point of contact. The partner never emails your client, never joins their calls and never appears in shared folders. If the partner needs platform access, it is best to give it through a user seat you control, so you can remove it at any time.

What a good brief includes

Most delays come from missing information, not slow coding. A short brief saves a round of questions:

  • The design file with all states: desktop, mobile and any hover or dark mode notes.
  • The email platform (Klaviyo, Mailchimp, HubSpot, Salesforce Marketing Cloud or a plain HTML file).
  • Which sections must be editable by the client's team.
  • Fonts, brand colours, link URLs and any tracking parameters.
  • The deadline, and whether the files should be uploaded or just delivered.

If your team designs in Figma, the Figma to HTML email handoff checklist covers the details developers need, such as image export sizes and mobile layouts.

What White-Label Partners Usually Deliver

  • Custom HTML email templates and modular template systems
  • Figma and PSD to HTML email conversion
  • Klaviyo flow builds and campaign templates
  • Email QA and Outlook rendering fixes
  • HTML email signatures for client teams

Some agencies start with one type of work, often template coding, and add flows and signatures later once the relationship is proven. A modular template is a good first project, because the client can reuse it for months and you can see the quality of the code up close.

Pricing Models

ModelHow it worksBest for
Per projectA fixed price for each template or flowAgencies with occasional email work
Monthly bundleA set number of emails each month at a lower rateAgencies with steady email demand
Dedicated capacityReserved developer time each monthAgencies running email for many clients

For typical template costs, see how much a custom HTML email template costs and our pricing page.

Setting your own margin

Your price to the client should cover the partner's fee, your project management time, client meetings and revisions you handle yourself. Many agencies price email work the same way they price design work: by the value to the client and the time spent on communication, not only by the partner's cost. Keep a simple sheet of partner prices per deliverable so your team can quote quickly and consistently.

How to Choose a White-Label Email Partner

  1. No branding: the partner's name should never appear in code, files or emails. Check HTML comments, image file names and upload folders.
  2. NDA: they should sign one on request and never contact your clients.
  3. Testing: ask which clients they test in; Outlook and dark mode should be included. Our testing checklist shows what good QA covers.
  4. Platform experience: Klaviyo, Mailchimp, HubSpot and Salesforce Marketing Cloud at minimum.
  5. Turnaround and communication: clear deadlines and fast replies in your time zone.
  6. A test project: start with one email before committing to volume.

If you are still deciding between building an in-house role and using an outside team, our comparison of hiring an email developer vs an agency walks through the trade-offs.

Red flags to watch for

  • A partner who asks to speak to your client directly "to save time".
  • Code full of builder output or classes named after another company.
  • No clear answer about which Outlook versions they test.
  • Vague revision terms, or extra charges for small text changes.
  • No written turnaround time.

A quick code check

When the first template arrives, open the HTML and look at a few basics. A clean file should use tables for layout, have Outlook conditional comments where needed, and carry no stray branding. For example, a well-built file often includes a block like this for classic Outlook:

<!--[if mso]><table role="presentation" width="600"><tr><td><![endif]-->

You do not need to read every line. You just want to see signs that the partner understands email rendering, not only web layout.

A Real-World Scenario

Picture a small Shopify design agency. A client who just launched a new store asks for a branded newsletter template and a welcome flow in Klaviyo. The agency has no email developer. They send the Figma file and a short brief to their white-label partner on Monday. The partner returns a tested, modular template on Wednesday and builds the flow in the client's Klaviyo account through a seat the agency set up. The agency reviews the work, asks for one change to the footer, and presents it to the client on Friday under their own name. The client sees a smooth project from one agency. The agency adds email to its service list and has a repeatable process for the next request.
