Short answer: in Mailchimp, go to Content, Email templates, Create template, Code your own, then choose Import HTML and upload your .html file or a .zip with the HTML and images. To let your team edit text and images later, the template needs Mailchimp's editable tags (such as mc:edit) added before import. Without them, every change means editing code.

Before You Import: Prepare the Template

  • Host images online or include them in the .zip. Local paths like C:/images/logo.png will break.
  • Add editable regions: put mc:edit="header_text" on text blocks and images your team will change. Each name must be unique.
  • Add repeatable blocks with mc:repeatable and mc:variant if you want to add or swap sections, like product rows.
  • Keep required merge tags: the footer must include *|UNSUB|* and your address tags, or Mailchimp will warn you.
  • Keep code lean. Heavy code can trigger Gmail clipping at 102 KB.
  • Inline your CSS. Mailchimp can inline CSS for you, but checking it yourself avoids surprises.

How Mailchimp's Template Language Works

Mailchimp reads special attributes in your HTML to decide what users can edit in the drag-and-drop editor. Here are the ones you will use most:

AttributeWhat it doesExample use
mc:editMakes text or an image editableHeadline, body copy, hero image
mc:repeatableLets users duplicate or remove a blockProduct rows, article blocks
mc:variantOffers alternative layouts for a repeatable blockImage left or image right
mc:hideableLets users hide a block without deleting itOptional banner

Example: An Editable Text Block

<td mc:edit="intro_text" style="font-family:Arial, sans-serif; font-size:16px;">Write your intro here.</td>

Example: An Editable Image

<img mc:edit="hero_image" src="https://example.com/hero.jpg" width="600" alt="Spring sale" style="display:block; max-width:100%; height:auto;">

Example: A Repeatable Product Row

<table mc:repeatable="products" mc:variant="Image left"> ... </table>

Put mc:edit on the elements inside the repeatable block too, so each copy can hold different content. Check Mailchimp's current template language docs, as supported attributes can change.

Step by Step: Import Into Mailchimp

  1. Open Content, then Email templates.
  2. Click Create template and choose Code your own.
  3. Select Import HTML and upload the .html or .zip file.
  4. Name the template and save it.
  5. Create a new email campaign and choose the template under Saved templates.
  6. Click each editable area to confirm it can be changed without code.
  7. Send a test to Gmail and Outlook before using it for real.

Mailchimp moves menu items from time to time. If a label has changed, look for the templates area and an option to code or upload your own.

Common Problems After Import

ProblemLikely causeFix
Can't edit anythingNo mc:edit tagsAdd editable regions and re-import
Images missingLocal file pathsHost images or upload them in the .zip
Layout breaks in OutlookDiv-based or modern CSS layoutRebuild with tables and Outlook fixes
Styles lostCSS in an external fileInline the CSS
Columns do not stack on phonesFixed widthsUse fluid tables and hybrid columns

If Outlook is the problem, read how to fix HTML emails that break in Outlook. For mobile issues, see why responsive emails fail on mobile, and for broken images, read why email images are not showing.

Planning Editable Areas With Your Team

Before adding tags, sit down with the people who will build campaigns. Ask them which parts change every send and which parts should never move. A good template gives them freedom where they need it and locks everything else.

  • Usually editable: headline, intro text, hero image, button text and link, product blocks and article blocks.
  • Usually locked: the header logo, the main layout tables, the footer structure and legal text.
  • Optional: banners and promo strips, marked as hideable so they can be switched off.

Give each mc:edit a clear name, such as hero_headline or product_1_price. Clear names make the template easier to maintain and easier to hand to a new team member. Also write a one-page guide that lists each editable area and its limits, such as the best image size or the maximum headline length. That guide prevents most of the layout problems that appear after launch.

Version Control

Keep the master HTML file outside Mailchimp, with a date in the file name. When you need a change, edit the master and re-import it as a new template. This way, you always have a clean copy to go back to.

Common Mistakes

  • Using the same mc:edit name twice, which makes Mailchimp mix up content.
  • Placing mc:edit on a table that holds the layout, so users can delete the structure by accident.
  • Editing the code after import without keeping a master copy outside Mailchimp.
  • Forgetting the footer merge tags, which blocks sending.
  • Uploading a .zip with images in nested folders that do not match the paths in the HTML.

Classic Builder vs New Builder

Mailchimp's newer email builder works best with its own drag-and-drop blocks, while custom-coded templates open in the classic editor. That is fine for most teams: the template keeps its exact design, and editable regions keep day-to-day changes simple. Our Mailchimp email templates service delivers templates already tagged, tested and imported into your account.

Starting from a design file? See our Figma to HTML email conversion service and the handoff checklist.

A Real-World Scenario

A team buys a newsletter template and uploads it to Mailchimp. It looks right, but the marketer cannot change a single word without opening the code. Every Monday, a developer has to edit the HTML by hand. The fix is to add mc:edit to the headline, intro, images and button text, and to make the article section mc:repeatable. After re-importing, the marketer builds each issue in minutes, and the design stays exactly the same. This is the setup we use for newsletter email templates.

Pre-Import Checklist

  • All image URLs are absolute or included in the .zip.
  • Every editable area has a unique mc:edit name.
  • Footer includes *|UNSUB|* and address merge tags.
  • CSS is inlined; the file is well under 102 KB.
  • Tested in Gmail, Apple Mail, Outlook and on a phone. Our email testing checklist lists the rest.

Moving between platforms? The process for Klaviyo is similar but uses different tags; see how to use a custom HTML template in Klaviyo. Agencies can also hand this work to us under their own brand through our white-label email development service.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I upload my own HTML template to Mailchimp?

Yes. Use Content, Email templates, Create template, Code your own, then Import HTML. You can upload a single .html file or a .zip that includes images.

Why can’t I edit my imported Mailchimp template?

The template has no Mailchimp editable tags. Add mc:edit attributes to text and image areas, then import it again.

Does Mailchimp support responsive custom templates?

Yes. Mailchimp sends your HTML as it is, so a well-built responsive template stays responsive.

Can I use a custom template with Mailchimp's new builder?

At the time of writing, custom-coded templates open in the classic editor. Check Mailchimp's current help pages, as this may change.

Can I let my team add or remove sections?

Yes. Mark those sections with mc:repeatable and, if needed, mc:variant for different layouts.

Can MailStora build and import a Mailchimp template for me?

Yes. We code, tag, test and upload templates into your Mailchimp account. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: Klaviyo supports three kinds of templates: drag-and-drop, full HTML, and hybrid. A full HTML template gives total design control, but only people who can code can change it. The best option for most stores is a hybrid template or HTML with editable regions: the layout is custom-coded, while text, images and buttons stay editable in Klaviyo's editor.

The Three Template Options in Klaviyo

TypeDesign controlEasy editingBest for
Drag-and-dropLimitedYesSimple campaigns
Full HTMLTotalOnly with codeFixed flow emails
Hybrid / editable HTMLHighYesMost brands

Drag-and-drop is fast and friendly, but you are limited to Klaviyo's blocks and settings. Full HTML lets you build anything, but every text change means editing code. Hybrid sits in the middle: a developer codes the structure, and marketers edit content visually. Klaviyo's features and names change over time, so check the current help centre for the exact options in your account.

How to Add a Custom HTML Template

  1. Go to Content, Templates in Klaviyo and create a new template.
  2. Choose the option to start from HTML (or code), then paste or upload your HTML.
  3. Upload images to Klaviyo's image library or host them on a stable CDN, and use full https:// URLs.
  4. Save, preview, and send tests to real inboxes.
  5. Use the template in a campaign or flow email.

Make sure your HTML is already email-safe before you import: table-based layout, inline styles, Outlook conditional comments and alt text on images. If it was built from a Figma design, our Figma to HTML email handoff checklist helps avoid surprises.

How to Make a Custom Template Editable

  1. Use editable regions: mark text and images with Klaviyo's editable attributes so they open in the visual editor. For example, a text area can be marked with <div class="editable" data-klaviyo-region="true">...</div>-style markup; check Klaviyo's docs for the exact current syntax.
  2. Build reusable sections: header, hero, product grid, testimonial and footer as separate blocks.
  3. Save universal blocks for the header and footer so one change updates every email.
  4. Use dynamic product feeds instead of hard-coded products, so best sellers and recommendations stay current.
  5. Add fallbacks for personalisation, for example {{ first_name|default:'there' }}.

Using event data in flows

In flows, the trigger event carries data you can loop over. In an abandoned cart email, for example, you can show each item with a loop like {% for item in event.Items %} ... {{ item.ProductName }} ... {% endfor %}. The exact field names depend on your integration, so check a preview with a real test profile. Always design a fallback for when an image or price is missing.

Common Problems

  • The editor changes your code: editing HTML in the drag-and-drop editor can rewrite it. Keep code edits in the HTML editor.
  • Layout breaks in Outlook: the template needs table-based code and Outlook fixes. See why emails break in Outlook and Klaviyo emails in Outlook.
  • Emails get clipped in Gmail: keep the HTML under 102 KB. See how to fix Gmail clipping.
  • Images look wrong in dark mode: see our dark mode email design guide.
  • Template tags show as raw text: a typo in {{ }} or {% %} syntax, or smart quotes pasted from a document. Retype quotes as plain straight quotes.
  • Broken images after import: relative image paths. Use absolute URLs.

Build Checklist

  • Max width 600 to 640px, table-based, role="presentation" on layout tables.
  • All key styles inline; media queries only as an extra.
  • Web-safe fallback fonts in every font stack.
  • Bulletproof buttons coded as live text.
  • Editable regions on every text, image and button that marketers will change.
  • Header and footer as universal blocks.
  • Personalisation tags with defaults.
  • Unsubscribe and address tags present in the footer.
  • Tested in Outlook, Gmail, Apple Mail and mobile. See our email testing checklist.

A Real-World Scenario

A fashion brand had a designer build a beautiful full HTML template. It worked well, but every weekly campaign needed a developer to change headlines and product images, which slowed launches. The template was rebuilt as a hybrid: the same design, split into coded sections with editable regions, plus a universal header and footer. The marketing team could now swap images, rewrite text and reorder sections in the visual editor, while the coded layout kept it stable in Outlook. You can see a similar layout in our fashion new collection launch email.

Where Custom Templates Pay Off

A branded system used across campaigns and flows keeps every email consistent: welcome series, abandoned cart, browse abandonment and post-purchase. Our custom Klaviyo email templates are built as editable modular systems, and our Klaviyo flow setup service puts them to work.

How to Plan a Modular Template System

Before any code is written, list the emails you send and the sections they share. Most ecommerce brands need a small set of sections that can be mixed and matched:

SectionUsed inEditable parts
Header with logo and navAll emailsLinks, logo (universal block)
Hero image and headlineCampaigns, welcomeImage, headline, button
Text blockAll emailsHeading, body text
Product grid (2 or 3 columns)Campaigns, flowsProducts via feed or event data
Review or testimonialWelcome, post-purchaseQuote text, name
FooterAll emailsSocial links, legal text (universal block)

With six to ten well-built sections, a team can create most campaigns without new code. It also keeps file size lower, because each section is lean and tested once.

Keep a short guide for the marketing team explaining which section to use for what, the recommended image sizes and the character limits for headlines. That small document saves many broken layouts later.

Maintaining the Template Over Time

A template is not finished on launch day. Email clients change, your brand evolves and new sections are needed. A few habits keep it healthy:

  • Keep a master copy of the HTML outside Klaviyo, in a shared folder or code repository, so you can always roll back.
  • Change universal blocks with care. An edit to the footer updates every email that uses it, including live flows.
  • Retest after big client updates, such as changes to new Outlook or Gmail, and after adding any new section.
  • Review flow emails every few months so old designs and expired offers do not keep sending.

Small, regular checks are far cheaper than a full rebuild when something breaks during a busy sale week.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use custom HTML in Klaviyo?

Yes. You can create a template from HTML in Klaviyo, or build a hybrid template with custom-coded sections that remain editable.

Will a custom HTML template work with Klaviyo's drag-and-drop editor?

Only if it is built for it. Templates with editable regions or hybrid blocks open in the visual editor; plain HTML templates only open in the code editor.

Can dynamic product blocks be used in a custom template?

Yes. Custom templates can include Klaviyo product feeds and event data, for example the items left in a cart.

Why do my personalisation tags show as raw text?

Usually a syntax error or curly quotes pasted from a document. Check the brackets and retype quotes as straight quotes.

Should flows and campaigns use the same template?

They should share the same design system, header and footer, so every email feels consistent, even if the sections differ.

Can MailStora build my Klaviyo templates?

Yes. We build editable Klaviyo template systems and test them in 50+ email clients. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: email images usually fail to show for one of seven reasons: the reader's client blocks images by default, the image path is local or broken, the image is on an insecure (HTTP) server, the file is too large, the format is not supported, Outlook ignores the size or a background image, or a firewall blocks your image host. Most of these are fixed in the template code.

Missing images make an email look broken, even when everything else is fine. The reader sees empty boxes, a red cross or a long line of alt text where your product photo should be. The tricky part is that images often work for you and fail only for some readers. This guide explains each cause, how to spot it, and how to fix it.

7 Causes and Fixes

  1. Images blocked by default. Some Outlook setups and company inboxes block images until the reader allows them. Fix: never put key text only inside images, and always write useful alt text.
  2. Local or broken image paths. A path like file:/// or C:/ only works on your computer. Fix: host images online and use full https:// URLs.
  3. HTTP instead of HTTPS. Many clients block images from insecure servers. Fix: host every image on HTTPS.
  4. Files too large. Heavy images load slowly or time out on mobile. Fix: keep most images under 200 KB and size them at twice the display width for sharp screens.
  5. Unsupported formats. SVG and WebP do not work everywhere. Fix: use JPG, PNG or GIF for email.
  6. Outlook sizing and background images. Outlook ignores CSS width on images and CSS background images. Fix: set the width attribute on the image and use VML for backgrounds. See background images in Outlook.
  7. Blocked image hosts. Company firewalls can block some file-sharing services. Fix: host images on your email platform or your own domain, not on Google Drive or Dropbox.

How to Find the Cause

Before changing code, work out which cause you have. A few quick checks narrow it down:

What you seeLikely causeFirst check
Images missing for everyoneBroken or local pathOpen the image URL in a private browser window
Images missing only in some work inboxesImages blocked or host blocked by firewallAsk one reader if a "download pictures" bar shows
Images missing in some clients onlyHTTP, SVG or WebPCheck the URL starts with https and the file type
Images slow or cut off on mobileFile too largeCheck the file size of each image
Image huge in classic OutlookNo width attributeLook for width="..." on the img tag
Background missing in OutlookCSS background onlyCheck for a VML fallback

To see the real image paths, open the sent email, view its source (in Gmail, "Show original"), and search for src=. Every path should start with https:// and point to a public server.

A Well-Built Image Tag

Most image problems disappear when every image in the template follows the same pattern. A safe image tag for email looks like this:

<img src="https://cdn.yourbrand.com/email/hero.jpg" width="600" alt="20% off all boots this weekend" style="display:block; width:100%; max-width:600px; height:auto; border:0;">

  • Full HTTPS URL on a reliable host.
  • width attribute so classic Outlook uses the right size.
  • Useful alt text that carries the message if the image is blocked.
  • display:block to remove the small gap some clients add under images.
  • max-width and height:auto so the image scales on phones.

If Outlook breaks more than your images, our guide on fixing HTML emails that break in Outlook covers tables, spacing and fonts too.

Design for Images Off

  • Use live HTML text for headlines, offers and buttons.
  • Give images a background colour so the layout still holds its shape.
  • Write alt text that tells the story: "20% off all boots this weekend", not "banner1.jpg".
  • Make buttons from code, not images. See bulletproof email buttons.

Designing for images off also helps screen reader users and people on slow connections. Our accessible email design guide explains how to write alt text that works for both. Image-only emails can also hurt inbox placement, which we cover in why emails go to spam.

Common mistakes

  • Putting the whole email, including the offer and button, in one image.
  • Leaving the file name as alt text, or no alt text at all.
  • Linking to images in a shared Drive folder that needs a login.
  • Deleting old images from the server, which breaks past emails still in inboxes.
  • Using a dark logo on a transparent PNG, which can vanish in dark mode.

Test Before You Send

Check every email with images off, in Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail. It is part of our 25-point email testing checklist. If images keep breaking, our email rendering fix service finds and fixes the cause, and our custom HTML email templates are built to work with images on or off.

Why Images Look Huge in Outlook

A related complaint: an image looks right everywhere except classic Outlook for Windows, where it appears at its full original size, for example a small headshot turning into a giant 2000 px photo. Outlook ignores CSS width and max-width on images and uses the file's real size instead. The fix is to always set the HTML width attribute (for example width="80") on every image, and to resize the file close to twice its display size. On high-DPI Windows screens, Outlook can also scale images unexpectedly; adding the Office DPI settings in the head (o:PixelsPerInch set to 96) keeps sizes stable.

A Real-World Scenario

A B2B software company sends a product update. Marketing sees every image in Gmail, but sales reps report that clients see empty boxes. The images were linked from a cloud storage share, which many corporate firewalls block, and the main headline was part of the hero image. The team moves all images to the email platform's own image library, adds width attributes and real alt text, and turns the headline into live text. The next send reads clearly in the same client inboxes, even for readers who never click "download pictures".

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are my email images not showing in Outlook?

Outlook may block images by default, ignore CSS image sizes or ignore CSS background images. Use width attributes, VML backgrounds and alt text.

Why do my images show in Gmail but not for some readers?

Those readers may have images turned off, or a company firewall may block your image host. Host images on HTTPS on your own domain or email platform.

What image format is best for email?

JPG for photos, PNG for logos and graphics with transparency, and GIF for simple animation. Avoid SVG and WebP in email.

Do large images cause Gmail clipping?

No. Gmail's 102 KB limit counts the HTML code, not image files. Large images slow loading, but clipping comes from heavy code. See our guide to Gmail clipping.

Why do old emails suddenly show broken images?

The images were probably deleted or moved on the server. Keep email images at stable URLs for as long as the emails may be opened.

Can MailStora fix images that don't load?

Yes. We fix image paths, sizing, Outlook backgrounds and alt text in existing templates. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: emails go to spam mainly because of three things: missing or broken authentication (SPF, DKIM and DMARC), low engagement from an old or bought list, and content signals such as image-only emails, broken HTML or a hidden unsubscribe link. Fix authentication first, then clean your list, then make sure your template is clean and balanced.

Spam filters do not look at one thing. Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook each weigh many signals: who you are, how people react to your emails, and what the email itself looks like. The good news is that most spam problems come from a short list of causes, and you can check each one in an afternoon. This guide goes through them in the order that usually matters most.

1. Authentication

Gmail and Yahoo require bulk senders to authenticate their domain. Without it, many emails go to spam or are rejected.

  • SPF: a DNS record listing the services allowed to send for your domain.
  • DKIM: a signature that proves the email was not changed. Set it up in your email platform with your own domain.
  • DMARC: a policy that tells inboxes what to do when SPF or DKIM fail. Start with p=none and monitor.
  • Send from your own domain, not a free Gmail or Yahoo address.

What the records look like

You add these as TXT records at your domain host. Your email platform gives you the exact values, but the shape is simple. An SPF record looks like this:

v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net ~all

A starter DMARC record, added at _dmarc.yourdomain.com, looks like this:

v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com

Once reports show your real sending services all pass, you can move to p=quarantine and later p=reject.

Common authentication mistakes

  • Two SPF records. A domain can only have one. Merge them into a single record.
  • Too many lookups. SPF allows a maximum of 10 DNS lookups. Old services left in the record can push you over.
  • Shared DKIM. Some platforms sign with their own domain by default. Set up a branded sending domain so DKIM aligns with your From address.
  • Forgetting other senders. Your help desk, invoicing tool and store platform may all send email as you. Each one needs to be covered.

If you have just set up a new sending domain, send volume slowly at first. Our guide to warming up a Klaviyo sending domain explains how to build reputation without a spam spike.

2. List Quality and Engagement

  • Never buy lists. Use double opt-in for pop-ups if spam sign-ups are a problem.
  • Stop sending to people who have not opened or clicked in 6 to 12 months, after a win-back attempt.
  • Keep spam complaints under 0.1%. Gmail's limit is 0.3%.
  • Add one-click unsubscribe; Gmail and Yahoo require it for bulk senders.

Inboxes watch how people treat your email. If many readers delete without opening, or mark you as spam, future emails are more likely to be filtered. Sending to fewer, more engaged people often gets more total opens than blasting the whole list.

Bot sign-ups are a growing problem for online stores. Fake addresses bounce, hit spam traps and drag down your reputation. See how to stop fake sign-ups in Klaviyo for form and list fixes.

Be careful when judging engagement by opens alone. Apple Mail Privacy Protection can make opens look higher than they are, so a list may seem healthy when it is not. Our article on open rates and Apple Mail privacy explains how to use clicks and orders as better signals.

3. Content and Template Signals

  • Avoid image-only emails. Use live text with images, not one big image.
  • Keep HTML clean. Broken tags and code pasted from Word look suspicious. Stay under Gmail's 102 KB limit.
  • Make the unsubscribe link easy to find. If readers can't find it, they click "Report spam".
  • Use real link domains that match your brand; avoid URL shorteners.
  • Write honest subject lines that match the content.

Content is rarely the only cause, but it can tip a borderline sender into spam. A single large image with no text gives filters nothing to read and gives readers nothing when images are blocked. If your images also fail to load for some readers, see why email images are not showing.

Template red flags

SignalWhy it hurtsFix
One big imageNo readable text, looks like classic spamLive HTML text for headline, offer and button
Heavy builder codeLarge file, Gmail clipping, messy markupLean hand-coded template
Tiny grey footerReaders report spam instead of unsubscribingClear, readable unsubscribe link
Mismatched link domainsLooks like phishingBranded click tracking domain
Misleading subjectHigher complaintsSubject that matches the body

Quick Fix Checklist

  1. Check SPF, DKIM and DMARC with a free DNS checker.
  2. Send a test to a Gmail inbox and use "Show original" to confirm SPF, DKIM and DMARC pass.
  3. Remove unengaged contacts and bounces.
  4. Review your template: text-to-image balance, code quality, footer.
  5. Run the 25-point testing checklist before each campaign.

A clean, hand-coded template helps with the content side. Our custom HTML email templates use lean code and live text, and our Klaviyo campaign management service includes list hygiene and segmentation.

Gmail and Yahoo Bulk Sender Requirements

Since 2024, Gmail and Yahoo apply stricter rules to anyone sending around 5,000 or more emails a day to their users. In short, bulk senders must:

  • Authenticate with SPF and DKIM, and publish a DMARC record (at least p=none) that aligns with the From domain.
  • Offer one-click unsubscribe in the email headers and process unsubscribes within two days.
  • Keep the spam complaint rate below 0.3%, and ideally under 0.1%.
  • Have valid forward and reverse DNS for sending servers (your email platform handles this).

Most platforms, including Klaviyo, Mailchimp and HubSpot, cover one-click unsubscribe for you. The part you must do is domain authentication. See our step-by-step DMARC setup guide for Klaviyo. Rules can change, so check Google's and Yahoo's current sender guidelines at the time you set things up.

A Real-World Scenario

A clothing store notices that its weekly campaign open rate has dropped sharply, and a few customers say the emails land in spam. The team checks "Show original" in Gmail and sees DKIM passing but signed with the platform's shared domain, and no DMARC record at all. They set up a branded sending domain, add DMARC with p=none, and send only to people who clicked or bought in the last 90 days for two weeks. They also replace a single-image sale banner with a coded headline and button. Over the next few sends, placement improves, and they slowly add the wider list back in. No single fix did it; the combination did.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why do my emails go to spam in Gmail?

Usually missing authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), low engagement or high complaint rates. Content issues like image-only emails add to the problem.

Do spam trigger words still matter?

Much less than before. Authentication, reputation and engagement matter far more than individual words, though misleading subject lines still hurt.

Does email design affect spam placement?

Yes. Image-only emails, broken HTML, hidden unsubscribe links and very heavy code are negative signals.

How long does it take to get out of spam?

It depends on the cause. Fixing authentication can help within days. Rebuilding a damaged sender reputation usually takes a few weeks of sending only to engaged readers.

Should I use a new domain if my emails go to spam?

Usually no. A new domain has no reputation and can perform worse. Fix the cause on your current domain first, then warm up volume slowly.

Short answer: an email looks broken on mobile when it has a fixed width, no viewport meta tag, columns that do not stack, or text and buttons that are too small. The fix is a fluid layout: tables with width="100%" and a max-width of about 600 px, columns that stack with media queries or a hybrid method, text of at least 14 px and buttons at least 44 px tall.

Signs Your Email Is Not Responsive

  • The reader has to zoom or scroll sideways.
  • Text is tiny and buttons are hard to tap.
  • Two or three columns squeeze next to each other.
  • Images spill past the screen edge.
  • Spacing looks huge on one side and cramped on the other.

Many people read email on a phone first. If the first view is hard to read, they often delete the email rather than zoom in. So mobile problems cost clicks even when the desktop version looks perfect.

Why It Happens

Email is not like a web page. There is no single browser. Each email client, such as Apple Mail, the Gmail app, Outlook for iOS and Samsung Mail, has its own rules about which CSS it supports. A layout that relies on one feature, such as media queries, may work in one app and fail in another. That is why good email code has more than one layer of protection.

6 Fixes

  1. Add the viewport tag: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">.
  2. Use fluid tables: width="100%" with a centered container of max-width:600px. For Outlook, wrap it in a fixed 600 px ghost table.
  3. Stack columns: use media queries to make columns full width under 600 px. For Gmail apps that ignore media queries, use the hybrid (fluid inline-block) method.
  4. Make images fluid: set width attribute plus max-width:100%; height:auto.
  5. Size text for phones: body text 14 to 16 px, headings 22 px or more.
  6. Make buttons tappable: at least 44 px tall and full width on mobile. See bulletproof email buttons.

Fix 2 in Detail: The Fluid Container

A typical container looks like this:

<!--[if mso]><table role="presentation" width="600" align="center"><tr><td><![endif]-->

<table role="presentation" width="100%" style="max-width:600px; margin:0 auto;">...</table>

<!--[if mso]></td></tr></table><![endif]-->

Phones get a table that shrinks to fit. Classic Outlook, which ignores max-width, gets the fixed 600 px ghost table instead. Without the ghost table, Outlook can stretch the email across the whole window. The difference between new and classic Outlook explains why this is still needed.

Fix 3 in Detail: Media Queries vs Hybrid

A media query stacks columns like this:

@media screen and (max-width:600px) { .column { width:100% !important; display:block !important; } }

This works in Apple Mail and many other apps. But some Gmail setups, such as certain third-party accounts in the Gmail app, may strip the style block. The hybrid method solves this. Each column is a div with display:inline-block, a max-width such as 300 px, and width:100%. When the screen is too narrow for two columns, the second one wraps below the first with no media query needed. Use media queries as an extra layer on top.

Fix 4 in Detail: Images

Write images like this: <img src="hero.jpg" width="600" alt="New spring range" style="display:block; width:100%; max-width:600px; height:auto;">. The width attribute keeps Outlook from showing the image at its full file size. The inline CSS lets it shrink on phones.

Why Builders Sometimes Get This Wrong

Some editors lock widths in pixels or produce nested tables that do not stack. Pasting designs from Canva or a Word document as one large image also breaks on mobile. A hand-coded, mobile-first template avoids these problems. Our responsive HTML email templates are tested on iPhone, Android and tablets, as well as desktop Outlook.

Another common cause is heavy code. When an email passes about 102 KB of HTML, Gmail cuts it off with a "View entire message" link, and styles at the end may be lost. See our guide to Gmail clipping at 102 KB.

Mobile-First Design Habits

Code can only do so much if the design itself does not fit a phone. A few habits at the design stage save a lot of fixing later:

  • Design the mobile view too. Ask for a mobile mockup, not only a desktop one, so the developer knows how each section should stack.
  • Keep the key message near the top. On a phone, the first screen shows only the header and a little more.
  • Avoid text inside images. It shrinks with the image and becomes hard to read.
  • Use generous line height. Around 1.4 to 1.6 makes body text easier to read on small screens.
  • Leave space around links. Links that sit too close together are easy to mis-tap.

When the design already follows these habits, the code stays simpler and there are fewer surprises across clients.

Common Mistakes

  • Setting width="600" on every inner table, so nothing can shrink.
  • Putting all layout CSS in the <style> block, so it fails when a client strips it.
  • Using a single image for the whole email, which makes text unreadable on a phone.
  • Forgetting height:auto, which stretches images out of shape.
  • Placing two buttons side by side with no room between them on small screens.
  • Testing only in a desktop browser preview instead of on a real phone.

Mobile Checklist

CheckTarget
Viewport meta tagPresent in the head
Container100% wide, max 600 px, ghost table for Outlook
ColumnsStack below 600 px, even without media queries
Body text14 to 16 px
ButtonsAt least 44 px tall
ImagesFluid, with alt text

A Real-World Scenario

A brand designs a two-column product grid in Figma and exports it through a drag-and-drop tool. On desktop it looks fine. On an iPhone, the two columns squeeze together and the prices wrap onto three lines. The developer rebuilds the grid with hybrid inline-block columns and a ghost table for Outlook. Now the products stack one per row on phones, keep two per row on desktop, and Outlook stays at 600 px. If you are starting from a design file, our Figma to HTML email service builds this stacking in from the start.

Test on Real Devices

Preview on at least one iPhone (Apple Mail and Gmail app) and one Android phone. Also check dark mode, since most phones use it. The full list is in our email testing checklist. For an example, see the fashion launch email in our portfolio, which stacks cleanly on every screen. The weekly newsletter email shows the same approach with multi-column content. If you also have Outlook problems, read how to fix emails that break in Outlook.

If you send through Klaviyo, our Klaviyo email templates are coded to stay responsive inside Klaviyo's editor too.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my email look tiny on my phone?

The email probably has a fixed width and no viewport meta tag, so the phone shrinks the whole desktop layout to fit.

Do media queries work in Gmail?

Gmail supports media queries in many cases, but not all Gmail apps and account types. The hybrid method stacks columns without media queries.

What width should an email be?

Around 600 to 640 px on desktop, and 100% width on mobile.

Why do my images overflow the screen on mobile?

They have a fixed pixel width in CSS and no max-width:100%. Keep the width attribute for Outlook, but add fluid CSS for phones.

Is a single-column layout better for mobile?

It is the simplest and safest choice. Multi-column layouts are fine if they stack cleanly on small screens.

Yes. We rebuild templates to be mobile-first and test them on real devices and 50+ clients. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: classic Outlook for Windows uses Microsoft Word to display emails, and Word ignores CSS background images. To show a background image there, add VML (Vector Markup Language) code inside Outlook-only conditional comments. Always set a solid background colour as a fallback and keep the text on top as live HTML text.

Why Outlook Drops Background Images

Outlook 2007 to 2021 and Microsoft 365 for Windows render HTML with the Word engine. It does not support background-image in CSS, so hero images with text on top show as a plain colour or a blank area. Apple Mail, Gmail, new Outlook and Outlook on the web show them normally.

This matters most for hero sections: a photo with a headline and a button on top. In classic Outlook, the photo vanishes. If the text is white and the fallback colour is also white, the headline disappears too. The reader sees an empty block at the top of your email. The difference between new and classic Outlook explains why the two versions behave so differently.

How the VML Fix Works

  1. Set the background image in CSS and with the background attribute on the table cell, for most clients.
  2. Inside <!--[if gte mso 9]> comments, add a v:rect with a v:fill that uses the same image, and a v:textbox to hold the content.
  3. Set the VML width and height in pixels; VML does not understand percentages well.
  4. Close the VML elements inside a matching <![endif]--> block after your content.
  5. Add the VML namespace to the <html> tag: xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml".

A Working Code Example

Here is the basic pattern for a 600 by 300 px hero. First, the table cell for most clients:

<td background="https://example.com/hero.jpg" bgcolor="#2b3a55" width="600" height="300" valign="top" style="background:url('https://example.com/hero.jpg') center / cover no-repeat #2b3a55;">

Then the Outlook-only VML that opens right inside the cell:

<!--[if gte mso 9]><v:rect xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml" fill="true" stroke="false" style="width:600px;height:300px;"><v:fill type="frame" src="https://example.com/hero.jpg" color="#2b3a55" /><v:textbox inset="0,0,0,0"><![endif]-->

Next comes your normal HTML content: the headline, text and button. Finally, close the VML before the cell ends:

<!--[if gte mso 9]></v:textbox></v:rect><![endif]--></td>

The color on v:fill is the Outlook fallback colour. The bgcolor and CSS colour are the fallback for everyone else.

Choosing the Fill Type

type valueWhat it doesBest for
frameStretches the image to fill the shapeHero images sized to match the shape
tileRepeats the imagePatterns and textures

With frame, export the image at the same ratio as the VML shape, or it will look stretched.

Rules for Safe Background Images

  • Always set a background colour close to the image's main colour, so text stays readable if the image fails.
  • Keep text as live text, not baked into the image.
  • Use fixed heights carefully: too little height cuts content off in Outlook.
  • Use it only where it matters, like the hero. VML adds code weight and counts toward the 102 KB Gmail limit.
  • Use absolute image URLs. Relative paths break once the email leaves your server.
  • Keep the image file small. A large hero slows loading on mobile data.

When Not to Use a Background Image

VML works, but it is not always the best answer. Sometimes a simpler layout gives the same result with less risk. Consider these options first:

  • Stack the image and text. Put the photo as a normal image and the headline below it on a solid colour. This works in every client with no VML at all.
  • Use a solid colour block. A strong brand colour behind the headline can look just as good and loads faster.
  • Use the image only on wider screens. On phones, a background image with text on top often gets cramped. Many teams hide it on mobile and show a plain colour instead.

Use a VML background when the design truly needs text over a photo, and when Outlook is a meaningful part of your audience. If your reports show very few classic Outlook opens, a clean fallback colour may be enough.

Working With Email Builders

Some platforms clean up code on import and may remove conditional comments or the VML namespace. After you paste or upload your template, send a test to classic Outlook straight away. If the image is missing, check whether the VML survived in the saved version of the code.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting the namespace on the <html> tag, so Outlook ignores the VML.
  • Opening the VML in one conditional block and never closing it, which can break the rest of the email in Outlook.
  • Using different image URLs in the CSS and VML, then updating only one.
  • Setting a VML height smaller than the content, so text is cut off.
  • Choosing a light fallback colour behind white text.
  • Letting an email builder strip the conditional comments when you paste the code in.

DPI Scaling and Dark Mode

On Windows laptops with display scaling above 100%, classic Outlook can scale VML shapes differently from the HTML around them. This can leave small gaps or a shifted image. Adding the Office settings block with o:PixelsPerInch set to 96 in the head helps keep sizes consistent. Dark mode is another risk: Outlook may change the fallback colour and text colour. Check the hero with dark mode on, and read our dark mode email design guide for safe colour choices.

Quick Checklist

  • VML namespace added to the html tag.
  • Image URL is absolute and the same in CSS and VML.
  • Fallback colour set in three places: bgcolor, CSS and v:fill.
  • Width and height in pixels, tall enough for all content.
  • Tested in Outlook 2016, 2019, Microsoft 365 and new Outlook.
  • Tested with images off.

These checks also appear in our full email testing checklist.

A Real-World Scenario

A retailer sends a seasonal promo with a lifestyle photo behind the sale headline. Their reports show a good share of opens on desktop Outlook, mostly from business addresses. In those inboxes, the hero shows as a plain white block with white text, so the offer is invisible. The developer adds VML with a dark navy fallback colour that matches the photo. Now Outlook users see the photo, and if images are off, they still see white text on navy. The e-commerce seasonal promo case study and our Black Friday sale email use this kind of hero.

Other Outlook Problems to Check

Background images are one of many Outlook quirks. Rounded buttons, spacing, fonts and DPI scaling also break. See how to fix HTML emails that break in Outlook and bulletproof buttons. If you need it done for you, our Outlook email rendering fix service repairs templates and returns before-and-after screenshots. The Canadian Choice case study shows a full Outlook rebuild. For new designs, our HTML email template development includes VML heroes where they are needed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Outlook support background images in emails?

Classic Outlook for Windows does not support CSS background images. Use VML inside conditional comments. New Outlook and Outlook on the web support CSS backgrounds.

What is VML in email?

VML is an old Microsoft vector format that the Word rendering engine understands. Email developers use it for background images and rounded buttons in Outlook.

Will VML affect other email clients?

No. VML sits inside Outlook-only conditional comments, so other clients ignore it.

Why is my VML background image stretched?

With type="frame", the image stretches to the shape size. Export the image at the same width-to-height ratio as the VML shape.

Can I use a background image on the whole email?

You can, but it is risky. Full-body VML is harder to control and adds weight. Most teams limit background images to the hero or one banner.

Yes. We add VML backgrounds with fallbacks and test in every Outlook version. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: a bulletproof email button is made from HTML and CSS, not an image, so it shows even when images are blocked. The most reliable method is a table cell with a background colour and a link inside it with padding. For rounded corners in Outlook, add a VML version inside Outlook-only comments. Make buttons at least 44 px tall so they are easy to tap.

Why Image Buttons Fail

Many email builders still let you drop in a picture of a button. It looks fine in the editor, but it causes real problems in the inbox.

  • When images are blocked, the button disappears and so does your click. Some Outlook setups and corporate filters block images by default.
  • Text inside an image cannot be recoloured in dark mode and is not read by screen readers.
  • Image buttons can look blurry on high-resolution screens.
  • Changing the wording means exporting a new image, which slows down every campaign.
  • Extra images add download weight and can hurt load time on slow mobile connections.

A live-text button avoids all of this. The text stays sharp, it can be translated or edited in seconds, and it works with accessible email design because screen readers announce it as a link.

Three Coding Methods

MethodHow it worksPros and cons
Padding on the cellColour and padding on the td, link insideWorks everywhere; only the text is clickable in some Outlook versions
Padding on the linkLink set to display:inline-block with paddingWhole button clickable; Outlook ignores the padding
VML buttonv:roundrect in conditional commentsRounded corners in Outlook; more code

Many developers combine them: a padded cell for the shape, border on the link to fill the clickable area, and VML for Outlook rounding.

Method 1: Padding on the Cell

This is the simplest and most stable pattern. The table cell holds the colour, and the link sits inside it.

<table role="presentation" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0"><tr><td bgcolor="#1a73e8" style="padding:14px 28px; border-radius:6px;"><a href="https://example.com" style="color:#ffffff; font-family:Arial, sans-serif; font-size:16px; text-decoration:none;">Shop the sale</a></td></tr></table>

The weak point is that only the words are clickable in some clients. A tap on the coloured edge does nothing.

Method 2: Border on the Link

To make the whole shape clickable, move the size onto the link. Outlook ignores padding on inline elements, but it does respect borders. So developers use a thick border in the same colour as the button.

<a href="https://example.com" style="background:#1a73e8; border:14px solid #1a73e8; border-left-width:28px; border-right-width:28px; display:inline-block; color:#ffffff; text-decoration:none;">Shop the sale</a>

This gives a fully clickable area in most clients, including classic Outlook, though line height can still vary slightly.

Method 3: VML for Rounded Outlook Buttons

Classic Outlook for Windows uses the Word engine, which ignores border-radius. If rounded corners are part of your brand, wrap a VML shape in conditional comments:

<!--[if mso]><v:roundrect xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml" href="https://example.com" style="height:48px; v-text-anchor:middle; width:200px;" arcsize="12%" stroke="f" fillcolor="#1a73e8"><center style="color:#ffffff; font-family:Arial, sans-serif; font-size:16px;">Shop the sale</center></v:roundrect><![endif]-->

Then wrap the normal HTML button in <!--[if !mso]><!--> and <!--<![endif]--> so Outlook shows only the VML version. The same VML approach is used for hero images; see our guide to Outlook background images with VML.

Button Design Rules

  1. Size: at least 44 px tall and 150 px wide; full width on mobile.
  2. Text: short and clear: "Shop the sale", "Book a call", "Track order".
  3. Contrast: at least 4.5:1 between text and button colour.
  4. One main button per email section, with a text link as a backup.
  5. Font: use a web-safe fallback so Outlook does not switch to Times New Roman.

On phones, a full-width button is easier to hit with a thumb. Use a media query to set the button table to width:100% under 600 px. If your layout does not adapt at all, start with our guide on why responsive emails fail on mobile.

Dark Mode and Buttons

Some clients invert or darken colours in dark mode. A light grey button with white text can end up nearly invisible. Pick a strong, mid-tone button colour that holds contrast on both white and dark backgrounds. Avoid pure black buttons, which can blend into a dark background. Test the button in Apple Mail, the Gmail app and Outlook with dark mode turned on.

Writing Button Text That Gets Clicks

The code makes a button work. The words make people want to press it. Good button text tells the reader exactly what happens next. "Shop the sale" is better than "Learn more", because the reader knows where they will land. Start with a verb, keep it to two to four words, and match the page the button opens. If the button says "Track order", the page should show the tracking details, not the home page.

Keep the label on one line on both desktop and mobile. Long labels wrap on small screens and make the button look broken. If you need extra context, put it in a short line of text above the button instead.

Accessibility Tips

  • Use real link text, not an empty link with a background image.
  • Do not rely on colour alone. The label should make sense on its own.
  • Keep enough space between two buttons so people do not tap the wrong one.
  • Add role="presentation" to layout tables so screen readers skip them and read only the link.

Common Mistakes

  • Using margin for spacing, which Outlook ignores.
  • Setting only border-radius and expecting Outlook to show rounded corners.
  • Putting the link only on the text, leaving the rest of the button dead.
  • Forgetting to update the link in both the VML and HTML versions, so Outlook users go to an old URL.
  • Setting a VML width too narrow, which wraps the text onto two lines.
  • Using vague labels like "Click here" that tell the reader nothing.

Quick Button Checklist

CheckPass when
Images offButton still shows with colour and text
Classic OutlookCorrect shape, font and full click area
MobileAt least 44 px tall, easy to tap
Dark modeText still readable
LinksVML and HTML links match and are tracked

A Real-World Scenario

A store sends a sale email with a rounded image button. In testing, the Outlook preview shows a blank space where the button should be, because images are off by default for that recipient. The team swaps the image for a padded-cell button with a VML fallback. Now the button shows in every client, the wording can change per campaign without a designer, and dark mode no longer hides it. This is the kind of button we use in our Black Friday sale email design.

Buttons are one item on our testing checklist. For other Outlook problems, read how to fix emails that break in Outlook. Every custom HTML email template we build uses bulletproof buttons, tested in 50+ clients. If you already have a template with broken buttons, our Outlook email rendering fix service can repair it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a bulletproof button in email?

A button built from HTML and CSS instead of an image, so it displays and works even when images are blocked.

How do I make rounded buttons in Outlook?

Use a VML roundrect inside Outlook conditional comments. Classic Outlook ignores CSS border-radius. New Outlook uses a web engine and shows border-radius normally; see new Outlook vs classic Outlook.

How big should an email button be?

At least 44 px tall so it is easy to tap on a phone, with enough padding around the text.

Why is only the text of my button clickable?

The padding is on the table cell, not the link. Move the size onto the link using matching borders so the whole area is clickable.

Can I use a custom font on a button?

Short answer: in Shopify admin, go to Settings, Notifications, Customer notifications, open Order confirmation and click Edit code. You can change the HTML and CSS, but keep the Liquid tags (like {{ order_name }} and the line-item loop) that pull in order data. Add your logo and colours first under Customize email templates, then preview and send a test.

Why Order Emails Matter

Order confirmations are among the most opened emails a store sends. They reassure the customer, cut "where is my order?" support tickets and are a chance to show your brand and recommend the next purchase.

Shopify's default template is clean and works, but it looks the same as thousands of other stores. A few careful changes make it feel like part of your brand, without risking the data that customers rely on.

Step by Step

  1. Brand settings: in Notifications, click Customize email templates to set your logo, logo width and accent colour. This updates all notifications.
  2. Open the template: Customer notifications, Order confirmation, Edit code.
  3. Back up the code by copying it into a text file before changing anything.
  4. Edit the HTML and CSS for layout, fonts and spacing. Keep all Liquid tags and loops.
  5. Preview with Shopify's sample data, then place a real test order to check discounts, shipping and taxes.
  6. Repeat for the shipping, delivery and refund notifications so all emails match.

Menu names in Shopify admin change from time to time. If you cannot find a label, search "notifications" in the admin search bar.

Understanding Liquid in Two Minutes

Shopify notifications use Liquid, a simple template language. There are two kinds of tags:

  • Output tags use double curly braces, such as {{ order_name }}. They print a value, like "#1042".
  • Logic tags use curly braces with percent signs, such as {% if %} and {% for %}. They decide what shows and repeat blocks.

Filters change how a value looks. For example, {{ total_price | money }} formats a number as currency. You can freely change the HTML around these tags. Problems start when a tag is deleted, or when an opening tag like {% if %} loses its closing {% endif %}.

Liquid Tags You Must Keep

  • {% for line in subtotal_line_items %} and its closing tag, which lists the products.
  • {{ order_name }}, {{ subtotal_price | money }}, {{ total_price | money }}.
  • Shipping and billing address blocks, and the order status link {{ order_status_url }}.
  • Conditions like {% if discounts %} that show discounts only when they apply.

Example: Restyling a Product Row

Inside the line-item loop, you can change the table markup around each product while keeping the data tags. A simple row might be:

<tr><td width="80"><img src="{{ line.image | img_url: 'compact_cropped' }}" width="64" alt="{{ line.title }}"></td><td>{{ line.title }} × {{ line.quantity }}</td><td align="right">{{ line.final_line_price | money }}</td></tr>

Copy the exact variable names from your existing template rather than from this example. Shopify's default code may use slightly different names or filters, and those are the ones that are known to work in your store.

Keeping the Whole Set Consistent

Customers see more than one email after they buy. A typical order sends a confirmation, a shipping update, sometimes a delivery notice and, now and then, a refund or cancellation email. If only the first one is branded, the others feel like they come from a different company.

A good way to keep them consistent is to build one shared header and footer and paste the same code into each notification. Keep a single master file with those pieces. When your logo or address changes, update the master file first, then copy it into each notification. Write down which notifications you have changed, so nothing is missed.

Which Notifications to Prioritise

  • Order confirmation: sent for every order, so start here.
  • Shipping confirmation: the second most seen, and it holds the tracking link.
  • Order cancelled and refund: sent less often, but tone matters when something goes wrong.
  • Abandoned checkout: if you use Shopify's version instead of a separate email platform.

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting an {% endif %} or {% endfor %}, which can break the whole email.
  • Testing only with sample data. Real orders with discounts, gift cards or local pickup can show blocks you never saw.
  • Using CSS that email clients do not support, such as flexbox for the main layout.
  • Adding large images that load slowly or fail. See why email images are not showing.
  • Putting a big promotion above the order details, which confuses customers.
  • Updating the order confirmation but leaving shipping and refund emails in the old style.

Ideas to Improve Them

  • A clear order summary with product images.
  • Help links: shipping times, returns, contact.
  • A small upsell or "complete the look" block, kept below the order details.
  • A dark mode friendly logo. See our dark mode guide.
  • A short thank-you line in your brand voice.
  • A large, easy-to-tap "View your order" button linked to the order status page.

Pre-Launch Checklist

CheckHow
Original code backed upSaved in a text file with the date
Liquid tags intactEvery if and for has a closing tag
Real test orderWith a discount code and shipping
Mobile viewReadable on a phone, no sideways scroll
Outlook and GmailLayout holds, nothing clipped
Other notificationsShipping, delivery and refund match

Shopify notifications are coded like other HTML emails, so Outlook and mobile rules apply. Use our testing checklist. If the layout falls apart on phones, read why responsive emails fail on mobile, and for desktop problems see how to fix emails that break in Outlook. Long orders with many products can also hit Gmail's 102 KB clipping limit, so keep the code lean.

A Real-World Scenario

A small clothing store edits its order confirmation to add a new header and a "you might also like" block. The preview looks good. A week later, a customer who used a discount code writes in: the email showed no total. The developer finds that an {% endif %} was removed during the edit, which hid the totals block for discounted orders. They restore the tag from the backup, move the upsell below the totals, and place real test orders with and without discounts before saving. This is why backups and real test orders matter.

Where MailStora Fits

For a finished example, see our order confirmation email design. Our transactional email templates service redesigns the full set, and our Shopify development team can handle the rest of the store. If you send post-purchase emails from Klaviyo, our Klaviyo flow setup service keeps those emails in the same style as your Shopify notifications.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I edit Shopify order confirmation emails?

Yes. Go to Settings, Notifications, open the notification and click Edit code. You can change the HTML and CSS freely.

Will editing the code break my order emails?

Not if you keep the Liquid tags and loops. Back up the original code and test with a real order after changes.

Can I use Klaviyo instead of Shopify notifications?

Klaviyo can send some order-related emails, but Shopify notifications are still used for core confirmations unless you set up a full replacement. Our comparison of Klaviyo vs Mailchimp for Shopify covers the wider choice.

How do I restore the default Shopify template?

Paste back the code you saved before editing. Shopify has also offered a revert option in the code editor; check the current admin for it.

Can I add product recommendations to the order email?

Yes, but keep them below the order details and keep them simple. The main job of this email is to confirm the order.

Yes. We design and code the full set of Shopify notifications with your branding. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: in HubSpot, open Marketing, Files and Templates, Design Tools, create a new file and choose Email template (coded). Build the layout in table-based HTML, then add HubL modules or a drag-and-drop area so marketers can edit content in the email editor. Include HubSpot's required tags for the unsubscribe link and company address, then test before publishing.

HubSpot's built-in email themes are quick to start with, but they limit how far you can go with brand design. A custom coded template gives you full control over the HTML while keeping the editor friendly for your team. This guide covers when to build one, the exact steps, sample HubL, common errors and how to keep the template easy to maintain. Menu names can change, so check HubSpot's current docs if a label looks different in your portal.

When You Need a Custom Coded Template

  • Your brand design cannot be built with the default themes.
  • You need exact control over Outlook and mobile rendering.
  • You want a set of reusable, locked brand modules for your team.
  • You send many email types (newsletter, product update, event invite) and want them to share one system.

Step by Step

  1. Open Design Tools and create a new coded email template.
  2. Paste your tested, table-based HTML layout.
  3. Add editable modules with HubL, for example {% module "hero_text" path="@hubspot/rich_text" %}.
  4. Or add a {% dnd_area %} so marketers can drag, drop and reorder sections.
  5. Build custom modules for repeated sections such as product cards or event details.
  6. Add required tags such as {{ unsubscribe_link }} and the company address.
  7. Publish, create a test email from the template and send tests to Outlook, Gmail and mobile.

A Minimal Template Skeleton

Here is the basic shape of a coded template. It starts with template annotations that tell HubSpot this is an email template:

<!-- templateType: email isAvailableForNewContent: true label: Brand Newsletter -->

Then a table-based wrapper, with modules in the editable spots:

<table role="presentation" width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0"> <tr><td align="center"> <table role="presentation" width="600"> <tr><td>{% module "logo" path="@hubspot/image_email" label="Logo" %}</td></tr> <tr><td>{% module "hero_text" path="@hubspot/rich_text" label="Hero text" %}</td></tr> <tr><td>{{ site_settings.company_name }} {{ unsubscribe_link }}</td></tr> </table> </td></tr> </table>

Check the current HubSpot documentation for the exact names of required tags and default modules in your portal, as these are updated from time to time.

Fixed Modules vs a Drag-and-Drop Area

Fixed modulesdnd_area
Layout controlDeveloper decides the orderMarketers can reorder sections
Risk of broken layoutsLowHigher if modules are not tested together
Best forStrict brand emails, transactional-style sendsNewsletters and campaigns that change often

Many teams mix both: a locked header and footer as fixed modules, with a drag-and-drop area in the middle for content.

Building Custom Modules

Custom modules are reusable blocks with their own fields. A product card module might have fields for image, title, price, and button text and URL. In the module's HTML you reference fields like {{ module.title }} and {{ module.button_url }}. Keep the HTML inside each module table-based and inline-styled, just like the main template, so it renders in Outlook. Our HubSpot email templates service builds this kind of module library for teams that send often.

Common Problems

  • Template won't publish: required tags are missing.
  • Editor shows no editable content: the template has no modules or dnd area.
  • Outlook layout breaks: the HTML uses divs or flexbox. See Outlook fixes.
  • Gmail clips the email: modules add code; keep it under 102 KB. See Gmail clipping.
  • Buttons look different in Outlook: use bulletproof email buttons rather than styled links alone.
  • Colors flip in dark mode: test and plan for it. See dark mode email design.

Adding Personalization and Logic

HubL also lets you personalize content and show or hide blocks. A greeting with a fallback might look like this:

Hi {{ contact.firstname|default("there") }},

You can also show a block only to certain contacts, for example:

{% if contact.lifecyclestage == "customer" %} ... {% endif %}

Use logic with care. Every condition is one more thing to test, and a typo can hide a whole section. Keep logic simple, give every personalization token a fallback, and send test emails as contacts with and without the data filled in. HubSpot's preview tool lets you view the email as a specific contact, which is a quick way to check this before you send.

If your HubSpot emails also go out as automated confirmations or receipts, the same rules apply. See our transactional email templates service for those builds.

Testing Before You Go Live

  1. Create a test email from the template and fill every module with realistic content, including long headlines.
  2. Send tests to classic Outlook for Windows, new Outlook, Gmail web and app, Apple Mail and iPhone.
  3. Check dark mode, images turned off and a narrow phone screen.
  4. Check the size of the sent HTML against the Gmail limit.
  5. Click every link, including the unsubscribe and preferences links.

Our email testing checklist covers each of these in more detail.

Keep It Maintainable

Name modules clearly, lock brand elements such as the header and footer, and document which modules to use for which email type. Our HubSpot email templates service builds coded templates and custom modules, tested and uploaded to your portal. For design handoff, use our Figma handoff checklist, and see what a custom build costs in our pricing guide.

  • Use labels that make sense to marketers, such as "Product card, 2 columns", not "module_7".
  • Keep one master template and avoid many near-copies.
  • Store the source HTML in version control or a shared folder so changes can be rolled back.

A Real-World Scenario

A B2B software company sends a monthly newsletter, product update emails and webinar invites from HubSpot. Each marketer has been cloning old emails and editing them, and the designs have drifted. Outlook users report broken columns. The team moves to one coded template with a locked header and footer, a drag-and-drop area in the middle, and a small set of custom modules: article card, feature highlight, event details and speaker row. New emails now start from the same template, and each module has already been tested in Outlook and dark mode. This kind of setup is similar to what we built in our SaaS onboarding sequence case study.

Frequently Asked Questions

Yes. Create a coded email template in Design Tools. Add modules or a drag-and-drop area so it stays editable.

What is HubL?

HubL is HubSpot's template language. It adds modules, variables and logic to HTML templates.

Why won't my HubSpot email template publish?

Usually required tags are missing, such as the unsubscribe link or company address.

Can I convert a Figma design into a HubSpot template?

Yes. The design is first coded as tested, table-based HTML, then split into HubL modules. Share the Figma file with notes on which parts should be editable.

Do I need a paid HubSpot plan for coded templates?

Design Tools access depends on your HubSpot plan. Check HubSpot's current plan details for your portal.

Yes. We build coded HubSpot templates and custom modules and test them in 50+ clients. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: An accessible email can be read and used by people with low vision, colour blindness, or who use screen readers. The main changes are useful alt text on images, text contrast of at least 4.5:1, real headings, body text of 14 to 16 px or larger, clear link text, live text instead of text in images, and layout tables marked with role="presentation".

Why Accessibility Matters

  • Millions of people use screen readers or zoom to read email.
  • Accessible emails are easier for everyone to read, especially on phones, in bright sunlight or when images are blocked.
  • In many regions, accessibility is a legal expectation for businesses. Check the rules that apply where you sell.
  • Clear structure and live text also help your email survive image blocking and dark mode.

Content Checklist

  1. Alt text: describe the purpose, like "Free shipping on orders over $50". Use empty alt (alt="") for decorative images, such as dividers and background shapes.
  2. Link text: say where the link goes. "Read the dark mode guide" beats "click here".
  3. Short paragraphs and plain language. One idea per paragraph.
  4. Don't rely on colour alone to show meaning, such as sale prices; add words or icons, like "Now $30, was $45".
  5. Clear subject line and preheader. Screen reader users hear these first, so make them useful.
  6. Avoid emoji overload. Screen readers read each emoji's name aloud, which can get long.

Good and bad alt text

ImageWeak alt textBetter alt text
Hero banner with sale textbanner.jpgSpring sale: 20% off all shoes this weekend
Product photoimageWhite leather trainer, side view
LogologoYour Store Name
Decorative dividerdivider line(empty alt)

Design Checklist

  1. Contrast: at least 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large headings. Light grey text on white is a common failure.
  2. Text size: 14 to 16 px body text, 1.5 line height.
  3. Left-aligned text for long paragraphs; avoid long centered text blocks.
  4. Buttons: large, high-contrast and coded as live text. Aim for a tap area of about 44px high. See bulletproof buttons.
  5. Dark mode: check contrast in both modes. See our dark mode guide.
  6. Spacing: leave room between links so they are easy to tap.
  7. Motion: keep GIFs subtle and avoid fast flashing.

Code Checklist

  • Add lang="en" (or your language) on the html tag.
  • Use real h1, h2 and p tags, not styled spans.
  • Add role="presentation" to layout tables so screen readers don't announce rows and columns.
  • Keep reading order logical when columns stack on mobile.
  • Set a title tag that matches the subject.
  • Use real data tables with th headers only for actual data, like an order summary.

Code example

A layout table and heading done well:

<table role="presentation" width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0"><tr><td style="padding:24px"><h1 style="margin:0 0 12px; font-family:Arial,sans-serif; font-size:28px; line-height:34px; color:#1a1a1a">Your order is on its way</h1></td></tr></table>

Compare this with a <span style="font-size:28px"> used as a heading. It looks the same, but a screen reader user can't jump to it with heading navigation.

Common Mistakes

  • The whole email as one image. Screen readers get almost nothing, and image blocking hides the message. See why email images don't show.
  • Alt text that repeats the file name or says "image of".
  • Many "Shop now" links with the same text going to different pages. Make each one specific, such as "Shop trainers".
  • Tiny footer text in light grey. Legal text still needs to be readable.
  • Columns that stack in the wrong order on mobile, so the image appears after its description.

Test It

Turn images off, zoom to 200%, and listen to the email with a screen reader (VoiceOver on Mac and iPhone, or NVDA on Windows). Check contrast with any free contrast checker. Accessibility checks are part of our email testing checklist.

  1. Images off: does the email still make sense?
  2. Zoom 200%: does text reflow without sideways scrolling?
  3. Screen reader: are headings, links and reading order clear?
  4. Dark mode: is every piece of text still readable?

A Real-World Scenario

A retailer sends a sale email where the main offer, the dates and the discount code are all inside one hero image. A customer using a screen reader only hears "sale banner" and a "Shop now" link. When the email was rebuilt, the headline, dates and code became live text on a solid background, the image got a short descriptive alt, and the button text became "Shop the spring sale". The email looked almost the same to sighted readers, but now worked with images off and with a screen reader.

Get Help

Every custom HTML email template we build uses semantic, screen-reader-friendly code, and our newsletter templates are designed for comfortable reading. Transactional emails matter too, since customers need to read order details clearly; see our transactional email templates. If your templates were made with AI, check them carefully, as they often skip this work; see AI-generated email templates.

Accessibility in Your Email Platform

Most email platforms let you add alt text and use headings, but you need to use these features on purpose. A few tips:

  • Klaviyo, Mailchimp and HubSpot all have an alt text field on image blocks. Fill it every time, or leave it empty on purpose for decorative images.
  • Use the editor's heading styles instead of making normal text bigger and bold.
  • Check the button block's colours against a contrast checker before saving it as a brand default.
  • Save accessible sections as reusable blocks so every new campaign starts from a good base.

If your template is custom-coded, the developer should set the lang attribute, heading tags and presentation roles once, so your team only needs to focus on alt text and link wording.

Quick Priority List

If you can only fix a few things this week, start here:

  1. Move key text out of images and into live text.
  2. Add meaningful alt text to every important image.
  3. Fix low-contrast text, especially grey text and footer text.
  4. Rewrite vague link text.
  5. Add role="presentation" to layout tables.

These five changes cover most of the problems readers hit, and none of them change the look of your brand.

Accessibility in Email Signatures and Plain Text

Accessibility is not only for marketing emails. Staff email signatures are often a single image with the name, phone number and logo baked in. That means a screen reader hears nothing useful, and the phone number cannot be tapped. A better signature uses live text for contact details and a small logo with alt text. Our HTML email signature design service builds signatures this way.

Also check the plain-text version of your emails. Some readers and some devices prefer it. Make sure it has clear line breaks, full link URLs and the same key message as the HTML version, not an empty or auto-generated mess.

Frequently Asked Questions

What makes an email accessible?

Useful alt text, good colour contrast, readable text size, real headings, clear link text and live text instead of text in images.

What is role="presentation" in email?

It tells screen readers that a table is used only for layout, so they read the content without announcing table rows and columns.

What contrast ratio should email text have?

At least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, following WCAG guidelines.

Should decorative images have alt text?

No. Use an empty alt attribute, alt="", so screen readers skip them. Do not remove the attribute completely.

How do I test an email with a screen reader?

Use VoiceOver on a Mac or iPhone, or NVDA on Windows. Open the email in a real client and listen from top to bottom.

Yes. We audit and rebuild templates with accessible design and code. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.
