Short answer: classic Outlook for Windows renders emails with the Microsoft Word engine, which supports very little modern CSS. New Outlook for Windows uses the same web-based engine as Outlook on the web, so it handles modern CSS much better. Microsoft is moving people to new Outlook, but many businesses will keep classic Outlook for years. For now, every email must work in both.

How the Two Engines Differ

Classic Outlook (Windows)New Outlook / Outlook on the web
Rendering engineMicrosoft WordWeb browser engine
CSS background imagesNo (needs VML)Yes
border-radius, max-widthNoYes
Media queriesNoPartial
MSO conditional commentsYesIgnored
Dark modeInverts coloursAdjusts colours

The simple way to think about it: classic Outlook is a word processor pretending to be a browser. New Outlook is a browser with some email-specific limits. Code that is valid in one can look very different in the other.

What Breaks Most Often in Classic Outlook

  • Width: max-width is ignored, so fluid layouts can stretch across the whole window unless you add a fixed-width ghost table.
  • Background images: CSS backgrounds disappear. You need VML, covered in our guide to Outlook background images with VML.
  • Rounded corners: buttons show as square boxes. See bulletproof email buttons for the VML roundrect method.
  • Spacing: margin and padding on some elements are ignored, and line height can add extra gaps.
  • Fonts: web fonts often fall back to Times New Roman unless you set a web-safe fallback in an MSO-specific style.
  • DPI scaling: on high-resolution screens, images and widths can scale unevenly.

What to Watch in New Outlook

New Outlook fixes most of the problems above, but it is not a normal browser. It filters some CSS and rewrites parts of your code, like other webmail clients. Some things to check:

  • Certain CSS properties and selectors may be stripped or rewritten.
  • Its dark mode adjusts colours on its own, which can change brand colours and logos. Our dark mode email design guide covers safe choices.
  • Your MSO conditional code is ignored, so the non-Outlook version of each element must look right on its own.

For a full list, read why new Outlook breaks some HTML emails.

What Is Happening to Classic Outlook?

Microsoft is making new Outlook the default for Windows and Microsoft 365 users, and older standalone Office versions have already left support. Classic Outlook in Microsoft 365 is still available, and large companies often delay switching. So the Word engine will stay in your audience for some time, even as its share falls. Check your own email platform's client report to see how many readers still use it. Timelines can change, so check Microsoft's current announcements before planning around a date.

How to Code for Both

  1. Keep table-based layouts. They work in both engines.
  2. Keep MSO fixes (ghost tables, VML backgrounds and buttons) inside conditional comments. New Outlook ignores them, so they cause no harm.
  3. Use progressive enhancement: rounded corners and modern CSS for new Outlook, with a clean square fallback for classic.
  4. Test both versions separately. They can look very different. New Outlook also has its own quirks; see why new Outlook breaks some HTML emails.

Example: One Button, Two Engines

A button can carry both versions in one block:

<!--[if mso]> VML roundrect for classic Outlook <![endif]-->

<!--[if !mso]><!--> HTML link with border-radius for everyone else <!--<![endif]-->

Classic Outlook reads the first part only. New Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail read the second part only. Each engine gets code it understands.

Example: Width Control

Wrap your fluid container in a fixed ghost table:

<!--[if mso]><table role="presentation" width="600"><tr><td><![endif]--> ... content ... <!--[if mso]></td></tr></table><![endif]-->

Classic Outlook holds the email at 600 px. New Outlook and phones use the fluid table inside. This also keeps your layout safe on mobile; see why responsive emails fail on mobile.

A Simple Plan for Teams

If you manage many templates, you do not need to fix everything at once. A step-by-step plan keeps the work under control:

  1. Check your data. Look at the email client report for the last few months. Note how many opens come from classic Outlook, new Outlook and Outlook on the web.
  2. List your templates. Start with the ones you send most: the newsletter, the welcome email and key transactional emails.
  3. Test each one in both versions. Take screenshots side by side and mark what breaks.
  4. Fix shared parts first. Headers, footers and buttons appear in every email, so one fix helps everywhere.
  5. Review again every few months. As more users move to new Outlook, your balance of fixes may change.

This approach avoids two extremes: dropping Outlook support too early, or spending hours on fixes that almost nobody sees.

Common Mistakes

  • Testing only in Outlook on the web and assuming classic Outlook looks the same.
  • Removing all MSO code after seeing a clean new Outlook preview.
  • Designing a hero that only works with a CSS background image.
  • Relying on a web font with no fallback.
  • Letting an email builder strip conditional comments on import.

Testing Checklist for Both Versions

CheckClassic OutlookNew Outlook
Layout widthFixed at 600 pxFluid, centered
Hero imageVML shows, fallback colour setCSS background shows
ButtonsVML or square, fully clickableRounded, fully clickable
FontsWeb-safe fallbackWeb font or fallback
Dark modeText readable, logo visibleBrand colours acceptable

The full process is in our email testing checklist.

A Real-World Scenario

A B2B company redesigns its newsletter and checks it in Outlook on the web. It looks perfect. After sending, the sales team, who still use classic Outlook, report a stretched layout, square buttons and a missing header photo. The fix is not a new design. The developer adds a ghost table, a VML hero and VML buttons inside conditional comments. The new Outlook view stays the same, and the classic view now matches. If your emails come from Klaviyo, the same issues appear; see why Klaviyo emails look different in Outlook.

Email signatures face the same split between engines. Our Outlook email signature service builds signatures that hold up in both.

When Can You Drop Classic Outlook Fixes?

Only when your own data says so. If classic Outlook is under 1 to 2% of opens and your audience is consumers, you can simplify. B2B senders should keep the fixes longer. Our Outlook email rendering fix service tests in every Outlook version, and our guide to fixing emails that break in Outlook covers classic Outlook in detail. The Canadian Choice case study shows a template rebuilt to work across Outlook versions.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between new Outlook and classic Outlook for emails?

Classic Outlook renders emails with Microsoft Word, which ignores most modern CSS. New Outlook uses a web engine like Outlook on the web and supports much more CSS.

Do I still need Outlook fixes in my email code?

Yes, as long as part of your audience uses classic Outlook. The fixes sit in conditional comments that new Outlook ignores.

Is classic Outlook going away?

Microsoft is moving users to new Outlook, but classic Outlook remains in use, especially in businesses. Check your own client data before dropping support.

How can I tell which Outlook my readers use?

Check the email client report in your sending platform. Some platforms group Outlook versions together, so a testing tool that separates them can help.

Does new Outlook on Mac use the same engine?

Outlook for Mac has its own engine and has never used Word for rendering. Test it as a separate client.

content:
Short answer: New Outlook processes your email before showing it. It can rename CSS classes, remove some head styles, change spacing and apply its own dark mode colours, so emails that depend on classes, embedded styles or tight spacing tricks are most at risk. The fix is to inline all important styles, avoid relying on class selectors, and test in new Outlook and Outlook on the web.

What Is New Outlook?

New Outlook for Windows is Microsoft's replacement for the classic desktop app. Unlike classic Outlook, which renders with Microsoft Word, new Outlook is built on the same web technology as Outlook on the web. That sounds like good news, and in many ways it is: modern CSS such as border-radius and max-width works much better. But it also means your email goes through a web-style sanitiser that rewrites the HTML before display. At the time of writing, many businesses run classic and new Outlook side by side, so you need to support both.

For a side-by-side comparison of the two engines, read new Outlook vs classic Outlook.

What Commonly Breaks

  • Head styles ignored or changed. Class names can be prefixed, so some selectors stop matching. A rule like .hero-title { font-size:32px } may never reach the element.
  • Media queries unreliable. Mobile layouts may not switch as expected, especially in narrow reading panes.
  • Spacing shifts. Default margins on paragraphs and headings can appear if you didn't reset them inline. Emails suddenly look loose or uneven.
  • Dark mode colours. Backgrounds and text can be adjusted, sometimes making logos or light text hard to see. See our dark mode guide.
  • Old MSO-only tricks. Layouts that only worked because of Word quirks can fall apart in the web engine, for example spacing done with empty paragraphs or mso-line-height-rule hacks without a proper fallback.
  • Unsupported selectors. Attribute selectors, sibling selectors and some pseudo-classes may be removed.

How to Fix It

  1. Inline critical styles: colours, fonts, widths, padding and margins on each element. Use an inliner as the last build step so you can still write clean CSS while working.
  2. Reset margins inline on p and heading tags, for example style="margin:0 0 16px".
  3. Use the hybrid method for columns so layouts stack without media queries. See responsive email fixes.
  4. Keep Outlook-only code in conditional comments so it only affects classic Outlook.
  5. Test in three places: classic Outlook, new Outlook and Outlook on the web.

Example: before and after

This relies on a class and will often break:

<style>.intro{font-size:18px;color:#333;margin:0}</style> ... <p class="intro">Welcome back</p>

This keeps working even if the head styles are changed:

<p style="font-family:Arial,Helvetica,sans-serif; font-size:18px; line-height:26px; color:#333333; margin:0 0 16px">Welcome back</p>

You can keep the class too, for media query overrides. But the default look should come from inline styles.

Example: Outlook-only code

Classic Outlook still needs ghost tables to hold columns. Wrap them so other clients skip them:

<!--[if mso]><table role="presentation" width="600"><tr><td width="300"><![endif]-->

New Outlook ignores this block, so it will not interfere with its web-based rendering.

Why It Looks Right, Then Changes

Some users report an email looking correct for a moment and then shifting. That happens when the client finishes processing styles after the first display. If your layout depends on head styles alone, the second pass can undo it. Inline styles solve most of these cases, because there is nothing left for the second pass to remove.

Quick Checklist

CheckWhy
All fonts, colours and sizes inlineSurvives class renaming
Margins reset on every p and headingStops default spacing appearing
Hybrid columns with max-widthStacks without media queries
MSO code in conditional commentsKeeps classic fixes separate
Logos tested on dark backgroundsHandles colour adjustment
Buttons coded as live textWorks in both engines

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting classic Outlook fixes. Classic Outlook is still widely used. Keep the fixes, just isolate them.
  • Testing only in Outlook on the web. It is close to new Outlook, but not always identical. Test both.
  • Using spacer paragraphs. Empty <p> </p> tags change height between clients. Use padding on table cells instead.
  • Relying on a template builder's preview. Real sends reveal processing that previews do not.

A Real-World Scenario

An agency sends a monthly newsletter for a client whose staff moved to new Outlook. The template was built with a big style block and short class names. After the switch, headings lost their size, paragraphs gained extra space and the two-column article section stayed side by side in a narrow reading pane. The fix was to inline all base styles, add margin resets and switch the columns to a hybrid layout. Classic Outlook ghost tables stayed in place inside conditional comments. The same template then looked consistent in classic Outlook, new Outlook, Gmail and Apple Mail.

If you use Klaviyo, many of the same issues show up there. See why Klaviyo emails look different in Outlook.

Get It Fixed

If you need fixes done for you, our Outlook rendering fix service sends before-and-after screenshots, and every custom HTML email template we build is tested in all Outlook versions. Agencies can use our white-label email development service to hand this work off. Before sending any update, run through our email testing checklist.

Dark Mode in New Outlook

New Outlook can change colours when a reader uses a dark theme. Light backgrounds may turn dark and dark text may turn light. Usually this is fine, but some elements suffer:

  • Dark logos on transparent backgrounds can disappear on a dark background. Add a thin light outline or a light padded background around the logo.
  • Text inside images does not change colour, so it can look out of place next to inverted live text.
  • Brand colours may be shifted slightly. Check that buttons still have strong contrast.

Test every template in dark mode in new Outlook, classic Outlook and Outlook on the web. They do not always apply the same changes.

A Simple Build Order

If you are building a new template that must work across all Outlook versions, this order keeps things simple:

  1. Build a single-column layout in tables with inline styles.
  2. Add hybrid columns where needed, using display:inline-block and max-width.
  3. Add ghost tables and VML for classic Outlook inside conditional comments.
  4. Add media queries last, only for polish.
  5. Inline, minify and check the file size.
  6. Test in all three Outlook versions, plus Gmail and Apple Mail.

Building in this order means that if a client strips something, the email falls back to a layout that still works, rather than breaking completely.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my email look different in new Outlook?

New Outlook processes email HTML before display and can change classes, head styles, spacing and dark mode colours.

Does new Outlook support media queries?

Support is limited and inconsistent. Use hybrid layouts that work without media queries, and treat media queries as an extra.

Should I remove my classic Outlook fixes for new Outlook?

No. Keep them in conditional comments. New Outlook ignores them, and classic Outlook still needs them.

Is new Outlook the same as Outlook on the web?

They are closely related and render in a similar way, but small differences can appear. Test in both.

Why is there extra space between paragraphs in new Outlook?

Default margins are applied when your head styles are removed or changed. Set margins inline on every paragraph and heading.

Yes. We test and repair templates for new Outlook, classic Outlook and Outlook on the web. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: Klaviyo emails break in Outlook mainly because classic Outlook uses Microsoft Word to render HTML and ignores much modern CSS. Common symptoms are images at full size, misaligned columns, Times New Roman text, cut-off lines and square buttons. Most can be fixed inside Klaviyo with set image widths, simpler blocks and web-safe fallback fonts; persistent problems need a custom-coded template.

Why Outlook Is Different

Gmail, Apple Mail and most phone apps use browser-like engines. Classic Outlook for Windows does not. It uses the Word rendering engine, which supports only a small part of CSS. It ignores things like max-width, border-radius, background images set in CSS, and many margin and padding rules on non-table elements. Klaviyo's drag-and-drop blocks try to handle this, but some settings and custom content still slip through.

New Outlook and Outlook on the web use a browser engine, so they behave better, but they have their own quirks. For the full background, see new vs classic Outlook and why new Outlook breaks HTML email.

Common Symptoms and Fixes

Symptom in OutlookCauseFix
Images huge or stretchedNo fixed widthSet a width in the image block and resize the file
Columns misalignedNested split blocksUse one split block per row, avoid nesting
Times New Roman textWeb font not supportedSet Arial or Helvetica as the fallback
Text cut or overlappingCustom line heightsUse line heights in pixels or 1.4 to 1.6
Square, broken buttonsCSS-only button stylesUse Klaviyo's button block, not a text link styled as a button
Gaps between imagesImage line spacingSet image blocks to display as block, remove padding

Images at full size

If you upload a 2400px wide image and don't set a width, Outlook may show it at its real size, far wider than the email. In the image block, set a fixed width (for example 600px for full width or 280px in a two-column row). Also resize the file before you upload. A smaller file loads faster and Outlook respects the width attribute more reliably. In custom code it should look like <img src="hero.jpg" width="600" style="display:block; width:100%; max-width:600px; height:auto" alt="New spring collection">.

Times New Roman fallback

Outlook does not load most web fonts. When the font stack is wrong, it falls back to Times New Roman. Always end your font stack with a safe font, for example font-family: 'Poppins', Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif. In custom templates, some developers also add an MSO-only style so Outlook uses Arial directly.

Cut-off or overlapping text

Outlook handles unitless or very tight line heights badly. Use pixel values that are at least 1.4 times the font size, for example 16px text with 24px line height. Avoid negative margins and very small padding around headlines.

Buttons that lose their shape

Rounded corners and padding on a link do not work in classic Outlook. Klaviyo's button block uses Outlook-safe code, so use it rather than styling a text link. In a custom template, use a bulletproof email button built with a table cell or VML.

Tips Inside Klaviyo

  • Preview with Klaviyo's inbox preview and send a real test to an Outlook account. Previews help, but a real send catches things previews miss.
  • Avoid pasting HTML into text blocks; it can carry styles Outlook can't read. Paste as plain text and style inside the editor.
  • Keep image text minimal; Outlook may block images by default. See why email images don't show.
  • Check dark mode, which Outlook applies aggressively. Use logos with a transparent background and a light outline if needed.
  • Avoid background images in blocks when the message depends on them. Classic Outlook may drop them. See Outlook background images.
  • Keep section widths consistent. Mixing 600px and 640px sections can cause odd gaps.

A Simple Testing Routine

  1. Build the email in Klaviyo and check the web preview.
  2. Run Klaviyo's inbox preview for Outlook 2016, 2019 and Microsoft 365 on Windows.
  3. Send a real test to a classic Outlook for Windows account and to new Outlook.
  4. Check at 100% and 125% Windows display scaling, as scaling can change spacing.
  5. Turn images off and check the email still makes sense.
  6. Switch Outlook to dark mode and check logos, text and buttons.

Our full email testing checklist covers the other clients too.

Common Mistakes

  • Fixing Outlook by trial and error in every new campaign instead of fixing the saved template.
  • Using a custom HTML block inside a drag-and-drop template with div-based code.
  • Testing only on a Mac, where Outlook uses a different engine from Windows.
  • Assuming that if Gmail looks right, Outlook will too.

A Real-World Scenario

A skincare brand sends a weekly product email from Klaviyo. Their B2B stockists mostly read email in Outlook at work. Each week the product grid breaks: the two-column split block has another split block nested inside it, so Outlook squeezes the text and pushes one product below the other. The fix was to flatten the layout to one split block per row, set fixed image widths and swap a styled text link for Klaviyo's button block. After that, the saved template stayed stable and the team stopped patching it every week.

When a Custom Template Is the Better Fix

If you keep fixing the same issues every campaign, the template itself is the problem. A hand-coded, editable template solves it once. Learn how in custom HTML templates in Klaviyo, or let us build it: our Klaviyo email templates are tested in every Outlook version and stay editable in the Klaviyo editor. If you already have templates you like, our Outlook rendering fix service can repair them instead.

What a Coded Outlook Fix Looks Like

When a template is coded by hand, a developer adds a few Outlook-only pieces that Klaviyo's blocks cannot always add for you. These sit inside conditional comments, so only classic Outlook reads them:

  • Ghost tables that hold columns at fixed widths, so a two-column row stays side by side.
  • VML code for background images and rounded buttons.
  • An MSO font rule that forces Arial when a web font is used elsewhere.
  • Line-height rules such as mso-line-height-rule:exactly, so text is not clipped.
  • Table cell padding instead of margins, since Outlook ignores most margins.

For example, a DPI fix helps when Windows display scaling is set above 100%, which can make images and tables grow unevenly. A developer adds an <o:OfficeDocumentSettings> block in the head with a PixelsPerInch value of 96. It is invisible to other clients and fixes a problem that is hard to spot until a customer reports it.

None of this is something you should need to think about every week. Once it is inside a saved template, every campaign built from it gets the same protection.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does my Klaviyo email look fine in Gmail but not Outlook?

Classic Outlook uses Microsoft Word to render emails, which ignores much of the CSS that Klaviyo's blocks and custom code rely on.

How do I test Klaviyo emails in Outlook?

Use Klaviyo's inbox preview and send a test to a real classic Outlook for Windows account. Also check new Outlook and Outlook on the web.

Can I fix Outlook issues without coding?

Many, yes: set image widths, simplify split blocks, use fallback fonts and Klaviyo's button block. Deeper issues need a coded template.

Why is my text showing in Times New Roman in Outlook?

Outlook can't load your web font and has no safe fallback. Add Arial or Helvetica at the end of your font stack.

Does Outlook on Mac have the same problems?

No. Outlook for Mac uses a browser-like engine, so it usually renders closer to Apple Mail. Classic Outlook for Windows is the main problem.

Can MailStora fix my Klaviyo templates for Outlook?

Yes. We fix existing templates or build new editable ones tested in 50+ clients. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: In Klaviyo, set up a branded sending domain (for example send.yourstore.com) under Settings, Domains, and add the DNS records Klaviyo gives you at your domain host to verify SPF and DKIM. Then add a DMARC TXT record at _dmarc.yourstore.com, starting with v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@yourstore.com. Monitor reports for a few weeks before moving to a stricter policy.

Why It Matters

Gmail and Yahoo require bulk senders to authenticate and publish a DMARC record. Without it, more of your emails land in spam or get rejected. Read the wider picture in why emails go to spam.

There are three pieces that work together:

  • SPF lists the servers allowed to send for your domain.
  • DKIM adds a digital signature so receivers can check the email was not changed and came from your domain.
  • DMARC tells receivers what to do when SPF or DKIM fail, and sends you reports. It also checks alignment: the domain in your From address must match the domain that passed SPF or DKIM.

Alignment is why the branded sending domain matters. If Klaviyo signs your email with its own shared domain, DKIM can pass but not align with your From address. A branded sending domain on your own domain fixes that.

Before You Start

  • Access to your Klaviyo account with admin rights.
  • Login for your DNS host (Shopify, Cloudflare, GoDaddy, Namecheap and so on).
  • A list of every tool that sends email as your domain: Klaviyo, Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, Shopify notifications, helpdesk, review apps.
  • An inbox to receive DMARC reports, ideally a dedicated address.

Step 1: Set Up a Branded Sending Domain

  1. In Klaviyo, open Settings, Domains and start the sending domain setup. Menu names can change, so check Klaviyo's help centre if yours looks different.
  2. Choose a subdomain such as send. or mail. so your main domain's email is separate. This protects your staff inboxes if marketing reputation dips.
  3. Klaviyo shows several DNS records (CNAME and TXT). Copy them exactly. A single missing character stops verification.

Step 2: Add the Records at Your DNS Host

  1. Log in to where your domain's DNS is managed (Shopify, Cloudflare, GoDaddy and so on).
  2. Add each record. Many hosts add your domain automatically, so enter only the host part if asked. For example, enter send rather than send.yourstore.com, or you may end up with send.yourstore.com.yourstore.com.
  3. On Cloudflare, set CNAME records to DNS only (grey cloud), not proxied, unless Klaviyo says otherwise.
  4. Return to Klaviyo and click verify. DNS can take from minutes to 48 hours.

Step 3: Add DMARC

  1. Check if a DMARC record already exists at _dmarc.yourdomain.com. Only one is allowed. You can look it up with any free DNS lookup tool.
  2. If none exists, add a TXT record: host _dmarc, value v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com.
  3. Read the reports (a free DMARC report tool makes them readable) to confirm all your senders pass.
  4. After a few clean weeks, consider p=quarantine, then p=reject.

DMARC tags explained

TagExampleWhat it does
vv=DMARC1Version. Must be first.
pp=nonePolicy: none, quarantine or reject.
ruarua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.comWhere daily summary reports go.
pctpct=25Apply the policy to part of failing mail, useful when tightening slowly.
spsp=nonePolicy for subdomains, if different.

A staged rollout might look like: p=none for a few weeks, then p=quarantine; pct=25, then p=quarantine, then p=reject. Only move on when reports show your real senders pass.

Common Mistakes

  • Two DMARC records. Receivers treat this as invalid. Edit the existing one.
  • Jumping straight to p=reject. A forgotten sender, like your helpdesk, will have its email rejected.
  • Two SPF records. Like DMARC, you can only have one SPF record per host. Merge them.
  • Typing the full domain in the host field on hosts that add it for you.
  • Setting up DMARC but still sending from the shared Klaviyo domain. Your emails may pass but not align.
  • Using a free email address as the From address, such as a Gmail address. You can't authenticate a domain you don't own.

Step 4: Warm Up and Monitor

A new sending domain needs a gradual warm-up. Start with your most engaged subscribers and grow volume over a few weeks. Follow our Klaviyo domain warm-up plan. Then keep your list clean; see how to stop fake signups. Keep an eye on open rates with care, since Apple Mail Privacy Protection can inflate them; see email open rates and Apple Mail privacy.

A Real-World Scenario

A Shopify store sets up DMARC with p=reject in one go after reading about the Gmail rules. A week later, customers stop getting replies from the support team. The DMARC reports show why: the helpdesk tool was sending as the main domain without DKIM set up. Moving back to p=none, adding DKIM for the helpdesk and waiting for clean reports solved it. Then they tightened the policy step by step.

Quick Checklist

  • Branded sending domain verified in Klaviyo.
  • One SPF record, one DMARC record.
  • DMARC starts at p=none with a report address.
  • Every sending tool listed and passing in reports.
  • Warm-up plan in place for the new domain.

Our Klaviyo campaign management and flow setup services include sending-domain setup and deliverability checks. Good authentication also pairs well with clean, light templates like our Klaviyo email templates.

How to Read DMARC Reports

Raw DMARC reports are XML files sent as email attachments. They are hard to read by hand, which is why most people use a free or paid report tool that turns them into a simple dashboard. When you look at the reports, focus on a few questions:

  • Which sources send as my domain? You should recognise every one: Klaviyo, your office email, Shopify and any helpdesk or review app.
  • Do they pass SPF or DKIM with alignment? For DMARC to pass, at least one of them must pass and align with your From domain.
  • Is there traffic I don't recognise? Unknown sources may be spoofing, or a tool someone on your team set up without telling you.

Fix each legitimate sender that fails, usually by adding its DKIM records or including it in your SPF record. Only when the reports are clean for a few weeks should you tighten the policy.

SPF Lookup Limit

SPF records can only trigger 10 DNS lookups. Every include: counts, and some includes contain more lookups inside them. If you add too many services, SPF can fail with a "too many lookups" error. Remove services you no longer use, and rely on DKIM alignment where you can. Klaviyo's branded sending domain handles its own SPF on the subdomain, so it does not add to the main domain's SPF record in most setups.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Klaviyo require DMARC?

Gmail and Yahoo require bulk senders to have DMARC, so in practice you need it. Klaviyo recommends a branded sending domain plus DMARC.

What DMARC policy should I start with?

Start with p=none to monitor. Move to quarantine and then reject only after reports show all legitimate senders pass.

Can I have two DMARC records?

No. Only one DMARC record per domain is valid. Edit the existing record instead of adding a second one.

How long does Klaviyo domain verification take?

Often minutes, but DNS changes can take up to 48 hours. If it still fails, check for typos and doubled domain names in the host field.

Should I use a subdomain for Klaviyo?

Yes. A subdomain like send.yourstore.com keeps marketing reputation separate from your main domain's day-to-day email.

Can MailStora set up my Klaviyo sending domain?

Yes. We set up branded sending, check authentication and warm up the domain. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

content:
Short answer: warm up a new Klaviyo sending domain by sending first to your most engaged subscribers only, then growing volume step by step over about 4 to 6 weeks. Keep flows on, because they go to active people, and slowly widen campaign segments from "engaged in the last 30 days" to 60, 90 and 180 days. Watch click, bounce and spam rates, and slow down if they get worse.

A warm-up is needed when you move to a new branded sending domain in Klaviyo, switch from another platform, or start sending again after a long break. This guide gives you a practical plan, the segments to build, the numbers to watch and the mistakes that most often cause trouble.

Why Warm-Up Matters

Inbox providers don't trust a new domain yet. A sudden large send looks like spam. Positive engagement early on builds a good reputation, which decides whether future emails reach the inbox.

Gmail, Yahoo, Outlook and Apple each watch how people react to your mail. Opens, clicks, replies and moving emails out of spam are good signals. Deletes without reading, spam complaints and bounces are bad ones. When your domain is new, the providers have little history, so the first few weeks carry a lot of weight.

Before You Start

  1. Authenticate the domain. Set up a branded sending domain in Klaviyo and add the DNS records it gives you. Make sure SPF, DKIM and DMARC are in place. A basic DMARC record looks like v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@yourdomain.com. See SPF, DKIM and DMARC for Klaviyo.
  2. Clean the list. Remove hard bounces, known bots and very old contacts with no activity.
  3. Build your segments (see below) before the first send.
  4. Check your templates. Light code, real text, working links and a clear unsubscribe link. Keep HTML under the Gmail 102 KB clipping limit.
  5. Set up Google Postmaster Tools for your domain so you can see Gmail's view of your reputation.

Segments to Build

Create a set of engaged segments with growing windows. Because Apple Mail can inflate opens, give weight to clicks, site activity and orders. For example, the 30-day segment could be:

  • Clicked email in the last 30 days, or
  • Opened email in the last 30 days, or
  • Active on site in the last 30 days, or
  • Placed order in the last 30 days, or
  • Created (joined the list) in the last 14 days.

Then duplicate it for 60, 90, 120 and 180 days. Exclude anyone who is suppressed or has bounced. Name them clearly, such as Warm-up | Engaged 30d, so nobody picks the wrong one mid-plan.

A 6-Week Plan

WeekWho to send toCampaigns
1Engaged in last 30 days2 to 3 sends
2Engaged in last 30 to 60 days3 sends
3Engaged in last 90 days3 sends
4Engaged in last 120 days3 to 4 sends
5Engaged in last 180 daysNormal schedule
6Full engaged listNormal schedule

Klaviyo can also run a guided warm-up for new domains. Either way, the principle is the same: engaged people first.

Treat the plan as a guide, not a fixed rule. A small list with strong engagement may move faster. A large list, or one with many older contacts, may need more time. If a week goes badly, repeat it instead of moving on.

What to Send During Warm-Up

  • Your best content: new arrivals, bestsellers, helpful guides.
  • Clear subject lines that match the content. Avoid tricks.
  • One main call to action per email.
  • A balance of text and images. Avoid emails that are one big image.

Do not use the warm-up for your hardest-selling or most discount-heavy messages to your oldest contacts. Save those for when your reputation is steady.

Keep Flows Running

Flows such as the welcome series and abandoned cart flow are triggered by recent actions. These people are highly engaged, so flow emails usually help your reputation. Leave them on. Pause or tighten winback flows that email long-lapsed customers until the warm-up is done.

Signals to Watch

  • Bounce rate under 1%.
  • Spam complaints under 0.1%.
  • Click rate steady or rising. Open rates are less reliable; see are open rates still reliable.
  • Gmail placement using Google Postmaster Tools.

What to do when numbers get worse

  1. Stop widening the segment. Go back to the last window that performed well.
  2. Check the last email for broken links, heavy images or a misleading subject line.
  3. Look for a bad source of contacts, such as a recent import or a form hit by bots.
  4. Check that your DNS records still pass authentication.
  5. Resume growth only after two or three healthy sends.

Common Mistakes

  • Sending to old or imported lists early. Clean them first; see stopping fake signups.
  • Skipping authentication. Set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC before warm-up.
  • Sending image-heavy or broken emails. Use a clean Klaviyo email template.
  • Jumping to the full list after one good week.
  • Building engaged segments on opens alone.

A Real-World Scenario

A home goods store moves from Mailchimp to Klaviyo in early autumn and wants to be ready for holiday sales. It sets up a branded domain, adds DNS records and builds the engaged segments. In week one it sends two campaigns to the 30-day group, while the welcome and cart flows run as normal. In week three, one send shows a jump in bounces. The team traces it to an old imported list that slipped into the 90-day segment, removes it and repeats the week. By the time the holiday calendar starts, the domain has several weeks of steady history. If you are still choosing a platform, see Klaviyo vs Mailchimp for Shopify.

Need a hand? Our Klaviyo campaign management service plans and runs warm-up with the right segments. For wider inbox problems, read why emails go to spam.

Warm-Up Checklist

  • Branded sending domain verified in Klaviyo.
  • SPF, DKIM and DMARC passing.
  • Google Postmaster Tools set up.
  • Hard bounces, bots and very old imports removed or suppressed.
  • Engaged segments for 30, 60, 90, 120 and 180 days built and named clearly.
  • Welcome, cart and post-purchase flows running; old winback flows paused.
  • Templates tested, light in code and free of broken links.
  • A simple sheet to log each send: segment, size, clicks, bounces and complaints.

Logging each send matters more than it seems. When something goes wrong in week three, a record of what changed makes the cause much easier to find. After the warm-up, keep sending mostly to engaged segments. Reputation is not built once and then kept forever. It moves with every send.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to warm up a Klaviyo domain?

Usually 4 to 6 weeks, depending on list size and engagement.

Can I keep my flows running during warm-up?

Yes. Flows go to people who just took an action, so they are highly engaged and help build reputation.

What happens if I skip warm-up?

Large sends from a new domain can land in spam or be throttled, and a poor early reputation takes time to repair.

Do I need to warm up if I change templates but keep the same domain?

No. Warm-up is about the sending domain and volume. A new template does not need one, but test it well before sending.

Should I send a big sale during warm-up?

Send it only to your engaged segments for the current week. Avoid emailing your full list until the warm-up is done.

Short answer: stop fake signups in Klaviyo by turning on double opt-in for your forms, adding form protection, and suppressing profiles that bounce or never engage. For low-quality real signups from big discount pop-ups, improve the offer and targeting rather than only raising the discount. Clean lists protect deliverability for everyone else on your list.

Fake signups are more than a nuisance. They cost money on contact-based pricing, they bounce, and they can include spam traps that hurt your sender reputation. This guide shows how to spot them, how to block them, how to clean up what already got in, and how to handle real people who join only for a code.

Why Bots Fill In Your Forms

  • List bombing: attackers sign a victim's address up to many lists at once to flood their inbox and hide other alerts.
  • Testing emails: bots check which stolen addresses are real.
  • Spam: scripts fill in any open form they find.

Whatever the reason, the result is the same for you: addresses that never engage, and sometimes complaints from people who never asked to join.

How to Spot Fake Signups

  • Sudden spikes in signups at odd hours.
  • Random strings as names, or the same pattern repeated.
  • Emails that bounce immediately or never open and never click.
  • Signups from countries you don't ship to.
  • Many signups from one form in a short time with no site browsing.

A quick check in Klaviyo

Open the list, sort by date added and look at the last few days. If you see a block of profiles added within minutes, with odd names like xkqjwpd and no Active on Site activity, that is almost certainly bots. Check the source field to see which form or integration added them.

Fixes for Bots

  1. Double opt-in: subscribers confirm by email before joining. Bots rarely confirm.
  2. Form protection: use Klaviyo's form settings and spam protection options; embedded forms on custom pages can add a CAPTCHA.
  3. Suppress bad profiles: build a segment of profiles with bounces or no engagement since joining, then suppress them.
  4. Check integrations: some fake signups come from checkout or third-party apps, not forms.
  5. Add a hidden honeypot field to custom-coded forms. Real people never see it, but simple bots fill it in.

A honeypot on a custom HTML form can be as simple as a field hidden with CSS:

<input type="text" name="website" tabindex="-1" autocomplete="off" class="hp-field">

Your form handler then rejects any submission where that field is not empty. Klaviyo's own sign-up forms have built-in protection, so this is mainly for custom forms that post to Klaviyo's API.

Setting up double opt-in

  1. In Klaviyo, open the list's settings and turn on double opt-in.
  2. Edit the confirmation email so it looks like your brand and has one clear "Confirm" button.
  3. Update the form's success message to say "Check your inbox to confirm."
  4. Start your welcome flow on confirmation, so only real people get it.

Cleaning Up What Already Got In

Build a segment such as:

  • Added to list in the last 90 days, and
  • Has not clicked any email since joining, and
  • Has not been active on site, and
  • Has not placed an order.

Review a sample by hand. If it is clearly bots, suppress the segment. Also suppress any profile that has hard bounced. Suppression keeps the history but stops sending, and in many cases suppressed profiles do not count toward billing. Check Klaviyo's current billing rules for your plan.

Fixes for Low-Quality Real Signups

Big "get 30% off" pop-ups attract people who only want the code. Some never buy or open again. Try:

  • A smaller offer plus a clear promise about content: new drops, guides, early access.
  • Showing pop-ups after engagement (time on site or scroll), not on arrival.
  • A strong welcome series that sorts engaged subscribers from code hunters.
  • A sunset flow that removes people who never engage after 90 to 180 days.

When judging engagement, remember that Apple Mail can make people look like openers when they are not. Use clicks, visits and orders too. See are open rates still reliable.

Why This Matters for Deliverability

Unengaged and fake addresses lower your engagement rates and raise bounces and complaints. That drags down inbox placement for your real customers. Pair list hygiene with proper authentication and read why emails go to spam. Our Klaviyo flow setup includes welcome and sunset flows that keep your list healthy.

If bots got into your list before a domain change, clean it first and then follow a Klaviyo domain warm-up plan with engaged people only.

Build a Sunset Flow

A sunset flow is your long-term defense. It catches both bots that slipped through and real people who lost interest. A simple version:

  1. Trigger: profile enters a segment such as "no clicks, site visits or orders in 120 days".
  2. Email 1: a friendly check-in with your best content or a small offer.
  3. Wait 5 to 7 days.
  4. Email 2: a clear "Do you still want to hear from us?" with a single button to stay subscribed.
  5. Wait 7 days, then suppress anyone who still has not clicked or visited.

Keep these emails light, with a clear button and plain text that works with images off. The goal is to give real people one last easy way to stay, and to quietly remove everyone else. Run the flow all the time, not as a one-off clean-up, so bad profiles never build up again. If your store runs on Shopify and you are still comparing platforms, see Klaviyo vs Mailchimp for Shopify.

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting profiles in bulk without checking a sample first.
  • Sending a winback campaign to the bot segment "just in case".
  • Turning on double opt-in but leaving the welcome flow triggered by list join, so bots still get emails.
  • Only fixing the pop-up and forgetting a footer form or checkout integration.

A Real-World Scenario

A beauty brand sees its list jump by a few thousand overnight. Revenue does not move, and the next campaign shows a spike in bounces. The source field points to an embedded footer form on an old landing page. The team removes the form, adds double opt-in to the main list, suppresses the new profiles with no activity and moves the welcome flow trigger to confirmation. The next campaign goes only to engaged segments while numbers settle.

Quick Checklist

  • Double opt-in on for public forms.
  • Honeypot or CAPTCHA on custom forms.
  • Welcome flow starts on confirmation.
  • Bounced and bot profiles suppressed.
  • Sunset flow running every month.
  • Clean, tested Klaviyo email templates for the confirmation and welcome emails.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why am I getting fake signups in Klaviyo?

Bots fill in exposed forms, sometimes to test stolen emails or to spam. Double opt-in and form protection stop most of them.

Does double opt-in reduce my list growth?

It lowers raw signup numbers, but the list is cleaner and more engaged, which usually improves revenue per subscriber.

Should I delete unengaged subscribers?

Suppress them after a win-back attempt. Suppressed profiles stop receiving emails but keep their history.

Do fake profiles cost me money in Klaviyo?

They can, because pricing is based on contacts. Suppressing them may help. Check Klaviyo's current billing rules for your plan.

Can bots get past double opt-in?

Rarely. They would need access to the inbox to click the confirmation link. Most bot signups simply never confirm.

Can MailStora clean up my Klaviyo list?

Yes. We set up forms, welcome and sunset flows and suppression segments. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: not on their own. Apple Mail Privacy Protection loads images, including tracking pixels, for many Apple Mail users whether they read the email or not, and some security scanners do the same. That inflates opens. Use click rate, conversion rate, revenue per recipient and unsubscribe rate as your main measures, and use opens only as a rough trend.

Open rate used to be the first number every marketer checked. Today it is one of the least trustworthy. This guide explains why, which metrics to use instead, and how to update your segments, tests and flows so they are not built on bad data.

How Open Tracking Works

An "open" is not really a read. Your email platform adds a tiny, invisible image to each email, often called a tracking pixel. It looks something like this:

<img src="https://track.example.com/o/abc123.gif" width="1" height="1" alt="">

When the email client downloads that image, the platform logs an open. So an open only means "the image was requested". Anything that loads images without a person reading the email counts as an open. Anything that blocks images hides a real read.

Why Open Rates Are Inflated

  • Apple Mail Privacy Protection preloads images, counting an open even if the email was never read. It applies to Apple Mail on iPhone, iPad and Mac when the user turns it on, and many do.
  • Security scanners in company inboxes open links and images to check them. B2B lists are often hit hardest.
  • Image blocking in some clients does the opposite, hiding real opens. Some Outlook setups block images by default. See why email images are not showing.

The result is noise in both directions. Your open rate can go up while real reading stays flat, and it can hide real readers too. Many platforms now try to flag machine opens, but at the time of writing none can separate them perfectly.

Better Metrics

MetricWhat it tells you
Click rateReal interest in the content
Placed order rateWhether the email drives sales
Revenue per recipientValue of each send, comparable across campaigns
Unsubscribe and spam rateWhether you are sending too often or to the wrong people
Bounce rateList quality and whether addresses still exist

Clicks can also be triggered by scanners, but far less often than opens. Revenue and orders are the hardest to fake. For ecommerce, revenue per recipient is often the single most useful number, because it lets you compare a big campaign with a small one fairly.

How to calculate revenue per recipient

Divide attributed revenue by the number of people the email was delivered to. If a campaign reached 20,000 people and your platform attributes a given amount of revenue to it, divide that amount by 20,000. Track this per campaign and per flow message over time. Keep your attribution window the same when comparing, or the numbers will not line up.

What to Change

  1. Segments: define "engaged" by clicks, site visits or orders, not only opens.
  2. A/B tests: judge subject line tests by clicks or revenue, not opens.
  3. Sunset flows: include click and order activity so Apple users aren't kept forever.
  4. Design for clicks: clear buttons and one main action per email. See bulletproof email buttons.
  5. Reporting: put click rate and revenue first in your dashboards, with opens as a secondary line.

Rebuilding an engaged segment

A common old segment was "opened at least once in the last 90 days". With inflated opens, that segment includes many people who never really read anything. A safer version combines signals:

  • Clicked an email in the last 90 days, or
  • Viewed a product or visited the site in the last 90 days, or
  • Placed an order in the last 180 days, or
  • Joined the list in the last 30 days.

You can still include opens for very recent activity, such as the last 30 days, if your platform filters out obvious machine opens. The key is not to rely on opens alone.

Fixing subject line tests

If you test two subject lines and pick the winner by opens, Apple preloads can make the result random. Pick by click rate or placed order rate. You may need larger test groups or longer test windows, because clicks are rarer than opens. That is fine. A slower, accurate result beats a fast, wrong one.

Better templates improve the metrics that matter. Our custom HTML email templates and Klaviyo campaign management focus on clicks and revenue. For warm-up segments that use these signals, see Klaviyo domain warm-up.

Where Opens Are Still Useful

  • Spotting deliverability drops. If open rate falls sharply at one mailbox provider, such as Gmail, it can mean you are landing in spam. Read why emails go to spam.
  • Long-term trends. A slow decline across months still says something, even if the exact number is inflated.
  • Non-Apple segments. Some platforms let you filter by client, so you can look at opens for non-Apple users only.

Common Mistakes

  • Celebrating a jump in open rate that came from a change in the audience's device mix.
  • Keeping unengaged subscribers forever because Apple preloads mark them as "openers".
  • Sending "we miss you" winback emails to people who are actually active buyers, because the rules only looked at opens.
  • Judging a welcome series by opens when the real goal is first purchase.
  • Letting bots stay on the list. Fake signups can add machine opens and clicks. See stopping fake signups in Klaviyo.

A Real-World Scenario

A fashion brand notices its open rate looks strong and steady, yet sales from email are slipping. When it looks closer, much of the list uses Apple Mail. The sunset flow only removes people with no opens in 180 days, so almost nobody is ever removed. The team changes the engaged definition to clicks, site visits and orders, and rebuilds the sunset flow around those signals. The list gets smaller, but sends now go to people who actually buy, which is better for deliverability and for cost on contact-based pricing.

Quick Checklist

  • Dashboards lead with click rate and revenue per recipient.
  • Engaged segments use clicks, visits and orders.
  • A/B tests pick winners by clicks or revenue.
  • Sunset and winback flows use more than opens. Our Klaviyo flow setup service builds them this way.
  • Each email has one clear call to action.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are my email open rates so high?

Apple Mail Privacy Protection and security scanners load tracking pixels automatically, which counts as opens even without a real read.

What is a good click rate for email?

It varies by industry, but ecommerce campaigns often see 1 to 3%, and flows usually higher. Compare against your own history rather than a general benchmark.

Should I still track open rates?

Yes, as a trend and for spotting deliverability drops, but don't use them as your main success measure.

Can I tell which opens are from Apple Mail?

Some platforms flag or filter likely machine opens. It is not perfect, so treat those filters as a helpful estimate, not an exact count.

Do inflated opens hurt deliverability?

Not directly. The harm comes when you use them to decide who to email, which can keep unengaged people on your list and lower real engagement.

Can MailStora help improve my click rates?

Yes. We design and code emails built around one clear action and test them across clients. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: Klaviyo is usually the better choice for Shopify stores that want advanced automation, deep segmentation and revenue reporting, because it syncs Shopify data in detail. Mailchimp can be simpler and cheaper for small stores with basic needs, or for businesses that also sell outside Shopify. Both charge by contacts, so check current pricing for your list size before you decide.

This guide compares the two platforms from the point of view of a Shopify store owner. It covers data, automation, segmentation, templates, cost and what it takes to switch. It does not try to crown a winner for everyone. The right tool depends on how much of your revenue comes from email and how much time you can spend on it.

Side-by-Side Comparison

KlaviyoMailchimp
Shopify dataDeep: products, orders, browsing, catalogAvailable via integration, less detailed
AutomationAdvanced flows with many triggers and splitsCustomer journeys, simpler
SegmentationVery detailed, predictive dataGood for basics
TemplatesDrag-and-drop, hybrid and HTMLDrag-and-drop and custom HTML
SMSBuilt inAvailable in some regions
Best forGrowing ecommerce brandsSmall stores, mixed businesses

Features and plans change often. Treat this table as a starting point and confirm details on each vendor's site at the time you compare.

How Each Platform Uses Shopify Data

The biggest practical difference is data. Klaviyo pulls Shopify events such as Viewed Product, Added to Cart, Started Checkout and Placed Order, along with product details like title, image, price and URL. You can use those events as flow triggers and as filters in segments. You can also drop product data straight into emails. For example, an abandoned cart email can loop over the items in the cart:

{% for item in event.extra.line_items %} {{ item.product.title }} {% endfor %}

Mailchimp connects to Shopify too and can sync customers, orders and products. It supports product blocks and abandoned cart automations. For many small stores that is enough. The gap shows up when you want very specific rules, such as "bought product A, has not bought product B, and viewed category C twice in 14 days".

Automation and Flows

Klaviyo flows can branch on almost any profile property or event. You can add time delays, conditional splits, trigger splits and A/B tests inside a flow. Common Shopify flows include:

  • Welcome series for new subscribers
  • Abandoned cart and abandoned checkout
  • Browse abandonment
  • Post-purchase thank you and review requests
  • Winback for lapsed customers
  • Sunset for people who stopped engaging

Mailchimp's customer journeys cover the basics, such as welcome and abandoned cart. The builder is friendly, but branching and data depth are more limited. If you only need two or three simple automations, that may not matter. If flows are a big revenue source, it will. Our Klaviyo flow setup service builds these core flows with tested templates.

Segmentation and Reporting

Klaviyo segments update in real time and can use predictive fields such as expected next order date and predicted lifetime value, where available for your account. Reporting ties revenue to each campaign and flow using an attribution window you can adjust.

Mailchimp offers tags, groups and segments, plus ecommerce reporting when the store is connected. It is fine for "customers who bought in the last 90 days" style segments. It is less suited to many layered conditions.

Templates and Design

Both platforms have drag-and-drop editors and accept custom HTML. The way editable regions work is different, so a template built for one will not simply work in the other.

  • Klaviyo uses its own template tags and editable regions. A custom HTML template can be made editable with <div class="klaviyo-editable"> style markup or built as a hybrid template. See our guide to the Klaviyo custom HTML template.
  • Mailchimp uses mc:edit attributes, such as <td mc:edit="body">, to mark editable areas, plus merge tags like *|FNAME|*.

Rendering is the same problem on both. Outlook, Gmail and dark mode do not care which platform sent the email. A well-coded, table-based template works on either one.

Cost

Both charge mostly by the number of contacts, with extra cost for SMS. At the same list size, Klaviyo is often more expensive. That said, cost should be judged against what the platform earns. A tool that costs more but runs flows that recover abandoned carts may still be the cheaper option in real terms. Price your actual contact count on both sites, and remember that unengaged contacts still cost money. Cleaning your list helps on either platform.

Choose Klaviyo If

  • Email drives a big part of your revenue.
  • You need flows like abandoned cart, browse abandonment and welcome series with product data.
  • You want revenue attribution per email and flow.
  • You plan to add SMS alongside email in one tool.

Choose Mailchimp If

  • You have a small list and simple newsletters.
  • You sell on several platforms, not only Shopify.
  • Budget matters more than advanced automation.
  • Your team wants the simplest possible editor.

A Real-World Scenario

Picture a Shopify store selling skincare. It started on Mailchimp with a monthly newsletter and a basic welcome email. Two years later, the list has grown, the catalog has dozens of products and the owner wants replenishment reminders timed to when a bottle runs out. They also want different welcome emails for people who signed up through a quiz. That kind of logic needs order data, product data and branching. This is the point where many stores move to Klaviyo. A store that only sends a monthly update and a few promos, on the other hand, may never need to move.

Switching Platforms

Moving from Mailchimp to Klaviyo means exporting contacts with consent status, rebuilding flows and recreating templates. Plan a domain warm-up for the new platform. We rebuild templates for both: Klaviyo email templates and Mailchimp email templates. To bring your own design into Mailchimp, see importing a custom template.

Migration checklist

  1. Export all contacts with consent fields and suppression lists. Never re-import unsubscribed people as subscribed.
  2. Connect Shopify to Klaviyo and let historical data sync.
  3. Authenticate your sending domain with SPF, DKIM and DMARC. See DMARC setup for Klaviyo.
  4. Rebuild flows first, starting with welcome and abandoned cart.
  5. Recreate templates and test them in Outlook, Gmail, Apple Mail and dark mode.
  6. Warm up the domain with your most engaged segment before large campaigns.
  7. Run both platforms briefly in parallel, then turn Mailchimp automations off so nobody gets duplicates.

Common Mistakes

  • Choosing a platform on price alone, then outgrowing it within a year.
  • Importing old, unengaged contacts and sending them a big campaign on day one.
  • Copying template HTML across platforms without changing editable tags.
  • Forgetting to switch off old automations, so customers get two welcome emails.
  • Ignoring theme or checkout changes. If your store also needs work, our Shopify development team can help alongside email.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Klaviyo better than Mailchimp for Shopify?

For most growing Shopify stores, yes, because of its deeper Shopify data, flows and segmentation. Mailchimp suits smaller or simpler setups.

Is Klaviyo more expensive than Mailchimp?

Often, at the same list size. Compare current pricing for your contact count and expected email volume, and weigh it against the revenue your flows can drive.

Can I move my templates from Mailchimp to Klaviyo?

The design can be moved, but templates need to be rebuilt or adapted for Klaviyo's editor and tags. Mailchimp's mc:edit areas do not work in Klaviyo.

Will I lose my subscribers if I switch?

No, as long as you export them with their consent status. Keep unsubscribed and bounced contacts suppressed on the new platform.

Can I use both platforms at once?

You can for a short transition, but running both long term usually means double cost and a risk of duplicate emails. Pick one as your main platform.

Can MailStora help me switch platforms?

Yes. We rebuild templates and flows on the new platform and test everything. Request a free quote and get a price within 24 hours.

Short answer: hire a freelancer for small, one-off projects on a tight budget. Hire in-house when you send a large, steady volume and need someone full-time. Choose an email development agency when you need reliable quality, fast turnaround, testing across many clients and cover for platforms like Klaviyo, Mailchimp and HubSpot, without the cost of a full-time hire.

HTML email is its own skill. It is not the same as building web pages. Email clients like Outlook still use old rendering engines, Gmail strips some CSS, and dark mode can flip your colors. So the question is not only "who is cheapest?" but "who can ship emails that work everywhere, on time, again and again?" This guide walks through the three options, what to ask, and the warning signs.

Comparison

FreelancerIn-houseAgency
CostLow per projectSalary and benefitsPer project or monthly
SpeedDepends on availabilityFast once hiredFast, with backup people
TestingVariesNeeds toolsUsually included
PlatformsOften one or twoYour stackMany
RiskSingle point of failureHiring and trainingLower, contract based

Option 1: A Freelance Email Developer

A good freelancer can be excellent value. You talk directly to the person writing the code, and prices are often lower than an agency's.

Works well when: you need one template, a quick fix or a small batch, and the deadline is flexible.

Watch out for: holidays, illness or a busy month can stall your project. Skill levels vary a lot. Some freelancers are web developers who also "do email", and they may not know Outlook quirks or dark mode fixes. Ask how they handle Outlook rendering problems before you hire.

Option 2: An In-House Email Developer

A full-time developer knows your brand, your platform and your calendar. They can react the same day.

Works well when: you send many campaigns each week, run complex flows and have enough work to fill a full role.

Watch out for: total cost includes salary, benefits, testing tools and training. Hiring takes time, and if that one person leaves, the knowledge can leave with them. Testing tools that preview emails in many clients are usually a paid subscription on top.

Option 3: An Email Development Agency

An agency gives you a team: developers, QA and often designers. Work is usually priced per template or per month.

Works well when: you need steady output without a full-time hire, you work across several platforms, or you have deadlines around launches and sales.

Watch out for: some agencies are generalists who pass email to junior staff. Ask who will build your templates and how they are tested. MailStora is a specialist in this area: we build hand-coded email templates and platform templates such as Klaviyo and HubSpot, tested in 50+ clients.

Questions to Ask Any Option

  1. Can I see live examples that work in Outlook and on mobile?
  2. Which email clients do you test in? Outlook, Gmail and dark mode should be included. See our testing checklist.
  3. Will the templates be editable in my platform?
  4. What is the turnaround and how many revisions are included?
  5. Who owns the code, and do you offer support after delivery?
  6. How do you handle accessibility, such as alt text, contrast and readable font sizes?
  7. How do you keep file size small enough to avoid Gmail clipping?

Red Flags

  • Templates built with divs, flexbox or a single image.
  • No mention of Outlook or testing.
  • Very low prices with no revisions or support.
  • Code generated by AI and not tested. See AI-generated email templates.
  • No portfolio of real, sent emails, only design mockups.
  • Vague answers about who owns the final code.

A Simple Test Task

If you are unsure, start with one paid template. Give every candidate the same design and brief. When it comes back, check:

  • Does the layout use tables, for example <table role="presentation" width="100%">, rather than divs for structure?
  • Do buttons still work when images are off? A bulletproof button uses a real link with styled text, not an image.
  • Is there a hidden preheader text line?
  • Does it stack properly on a phone?
  • Does it look right in dark mode and in classic Outlook for Windows?
  • Can your team edit text and images in your platform without breaking it?

This one test tells you more than any sales call.

A Real-World Scenario

A growing online store has a marketer who builds campaigns in a drag-and-drop editor. Black Friday is coming, and the team wants a custom modular template, a new abandoned cart design and a fixed order confirmation. The workload is too big for the marketer, but not big enough for a full-time hire. A freelancer is booked up for November. In this case an agency makes sense: a fixed scope, a fixed deadline, testing included and people available if something breaks the week of the sale. After the season, the store can drop back to occasional work.

Cost Thinking

Compare total cost, not only the quote. A cheap template that breaks in Outlook costs you in lost clicks and extra fixes. An in-house hire costs salary even in quiet months. An agency costs more per hour than a freelancer, but often less than a full-time role, and it removes the single-point-of-failure risk.

For typical costs, read how much a custom HTML email template costs, and compare options in best email template development agencies. Agencies that resell email work can also use a white-label partner. MailStora offers hand-coded email templates from $40 with testing in 50+ clients; see pricing, or browse our portfolio.

How to Brief Whoever You Hire

A clear brief saves time and revisions with any option. Include:

  • The design file, such as Figma, with desktop and mobile views.
  • The platform the template will live in, such as Klaviyo, Mailchimp or HubSpot.
  • Which parts must be editable by your team, and which should be locked.
  • Brand fonts, colors and any fallback fonts you accept.
  • The email clients that matter most to your audience.
  • Your deadline and who will approve the final version.

If your design team works in Figma, share our Figma to HTML email handoff checklist with them first. It covers widths, spacing, image exports and the notes a developer needs. A good developer or agency will also ask questions back. If nobody asks about Outlook, dark mode or editing, treat that as a warning sign.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost to hire an email developer?

Freelance rates and agency prices vary widely. Custom templates commonly range from about $40 for simple builds to several hundred dollars for complex modular systems.

Is it better to hire a freelancer or an agency for email templates?

A freelancer suits small one-off jobs. An agency suits ongoing work, tight deadlines and projects that need broad testing and platform knowledge.

What should an email developer deliver?

Tested, responsive, table-based HTML that is editable in your platform, plus test screenshots and support for fixes.

When does an in-house email developer make sense?

When you have enough steady email work to keep one person busy full-time, and budget for testing tools and training.

Can a web developer build my HTML emails?

Some can, but email needs different techniques, such as table layouts and inline styles. Ask for tested email examples before you hire.

Short answer: AI tools can give you a good starting point, but the HTML often breaks in real inboxes. Common problems are div and flexbox layouts, missing Outlook code, styles left in the head instead of inline, large file sizes and no dark mode handling. Use AI output for ideas and drafts; production templates still need email-specific coding and testing.

Why AI Email Code Breaks

Most AI models learned HTML from websites. Email is a different world. Email clients use older, stricter and very different rendering engines, and each one strips or rewrites code in its own way. So an AI tool will often produce code that looks perfect in a browser preview and then falls apart in an inbox. Here are the most common reasons.

  • Web layouts, not email layouts. Flexbox and grid work in browsers but not in classic Outlook, which uses Microsoft Word to render HTML. Columns collapse, widths are ignored and elements stack in odd ways.
  • No MSO fixes. Ghost tables, VML backgrounds and bulletproof buttons are usually missing. See background images in Outlook and bulletproof email buttons.
  • Styles not inlined. Some clients strip or change head styles. AI tools often write a neat <style> block and a few classes, which is exactly what gets lost. See new Outlook issues.
  • Heavy code that pushes past Gmail's 102 KB limit. Repeated wrappers, comments and unused CSS add up fast.
  • No dark mode or accessibility work. Logos disappear on dark backgrounds, and images have empty or missing alt text. See dark mode and accessible email design.
  • Not platform-ready. Missing Klaviyo, Mailchimp or HubSpot editable tags, so your marketing team cannot change text or images without touching code.

A typical example

Ask a chatbot for a two-column product email and you may get something like this:

<div style="display:flex; gap:20px"><div class="col">...</div><div class="col">...</div></div>

It looks fine in Chrome. In classic Outlook, display:flex and gap are ignored, so the two columns stack at full width. In some webmail clients the .col class is renamed and its styles never apply. An email-safe version uses a table with fixed widths and inline styles:

<table role="presentation" width="600" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0"><tr><td width="290" valign="top" style="padding:0 10px 0 0">...</td><td width="290" valign="top">...</td></tr></table>

For mobile stacking you then add a hybrid or media query approach, plus an Outlook ghost table. That extra layer is what most AI drafts leave out.

How to Use AI Well

AI is not useless for email. It is fast, and it is good at some parts of the job. The trick is to use it where it is strong and check it where it is weak.

  1. Ask for table-based HTML with inline styles and Outlook conditional comments. Say it plainly in your prompt: "Use nested tables, no flexbox or grid, inline all CSS, max width 600px, include MSO conditional comments."
  2. Use AI for copy, subject lines and layout ideas, where it helps most. It can give you ten subject lines or three hero headline options in seconds.
  3. Run the output through an inliner and check the file size. Remove comments and unused styles before you send.
  4. Test in classic Outlook, Gmail, Apple Mail and on mobile with our testing checklist.
  5. Add your platform's editable tags so the team can edit it later. In Klaviyo, see custom HTML templates in Klaviyo.

A clear prompt gives a cleaner first draft. Something like: "Write an HTML email for a 600px layout. Use only tables for layout with role="presentation". Inline all CSS. Use web-safe fonts with fallbacks. Add alt text for every image. Include a bulletproof button that works in Outlook. Keep the file under 60 KB." This will not make the code perfect, but it avoids many basic mistakes.

Common Mistakes When Shipping AI Templates

  • Trusting the browser preview. A browser is not an email client. Always send real tests.
  • Copying text into images. Some AI design tools output the whole email as one image. It will be blocked by default in some clients, is bad for accessibility and can hurt deliverability.
  • Forgetting the plain-text part. Many platforms create it for you, but check it reads well.
  • Pasting code into a drag-and-drop text block. The editor may rewrite it and break the layout.
  • Skipping links and tracking checks. AI often leaves placeholder links like href="#".

Frequently Asked Questions

Can ChatGPT or other AI tools make HTML email templates?

They can create a draft, but the code often lacks Outlook support, inline styles and platform tags, so it needs fixing and testing before you send it to customers.

Why does my AI-generated email break in Outlook?

It usually uses divs, flexbox or modern CSS that classic Outlook's Word engine does not support. Tables, fixed widths and conditional comments are needed.

Is AI going to replace email developers?

AI speeds up drafts and copy, but reliable rendering across clients still needs email-specific knowledge and testing in real inboxes.

How can I make AI produce better email code?

Ask for table-based layouts, inline CSS, a 600px width, alt text and Outlook conditional comments. Then inline, check the file size and test anyway.

Is it safe to send an email that is one big image?

It is not a good idea. Images can be blocked, screen readers cannot read them, and image-only emails can look like spam. Use live text for key messages.
